102990.e: The male blackbird is black and has a yellow beak. It likes to sing from high places such as roofs.
102990.m: The blackbird has a yellow beak and sings beautifully.

102991.e: Pigeons make a deep cooing sound. You often hear it in towns.

a: Listening to recordings of bird calls
102992.e: There are recordings and apps with bird calls. If you listen often, you will soon recognise birds by their song.
102992.m: If you listen often, you learn to recognise birdsong.

102993.q: How do you behave if you want to listen to birds?
102993.e: Noise drowns out the song and scares the birds away. If you are quiet, you hear much more.
102993.m: Keep quiet if you want to listen to birds.

102994.q: What do you often count to identify a flower?
102994.e: Many kinds of flower have a fixed number of petals. That helps with identifying them.
102994.m: The number of petals helps you identify a flower.

102995.q: Which part of a flowering plant is especially helpful for identifying it, because it is often colourful?
102995.e: The flower has a typical colour and shape. That is why you look at the flower first when identifying a plant.
102995.m: When identifying, look at the flower first.

102996.q: What do you do with an unknown plant instead of pulling it up?
a: You photograph it and identify it later
You eat a piece of it
102996.e: A photo shows the plant exactly. At home you can identify it in peace, and the plant stays where it is.
102996.m: Photograph unknown plants instead of pulling them up.

102997.q: Which forest plant has large fronds and no flowers at all?
102997.e: Ferns don't make flowers. They spread with tiny spores that sit under the fronds.
102997.m: Ferns have fronds and no flowers.

102998.q: Apart from the flower, what else do you look at when identifying a plant?
102998.e: Each kind of plant has leaves with a particular shape. That is why the leaves are an important feature.
102998.m: The shape of the leaves also helps with identifying.

102999.q: How do you recognise a conifer?
a: By its needles instead of broad leaves
102999.e: Conifers such as fir and spruce have narrow needles. Deciduous trees have broad leaves.
102999.m: Conifers have needles instead of broad leaves.

103000.q: How do you recognise grass in a meadow?
103000.e: Grasses have long, narrow leaves. They grow close together and form the green meadow.

103001.q: What kind of leaves does a maple have?
a: Leaves with several points like a hand
103001.e: A maple leaf usually has five points. It looks a little like an open hand.
103001.m: A maple leaf looks like an open hand.

103002.q: Why don't you eat unknown berries in the forest?
103002.e: Some berries look tasty but are poisonous. Only eat berries that an adult knows for sure.
103002.m: Don't eat unknown berries, they can be poisonous.

103003.q: How do you behave when photographing animals?
a: With the flash right in their face
103003.e: Animals get frightened easily. If you are quiet and keep your distance, you don't disturb them.
103003.m: Photograph animals quietly and from a distance.

103004.q: What do you use to bring an animal closer in a photo without going closer?
103004.e: With the zoom, the camera can enlarge faraway things. That way you keep your distance.
103004.m: With the zoom you bring animals closer without disturbing them.

103005.q: Why do nature photographers like taking pictures early in the morning?
a: The light is soft and many animals are awake
Because the camera is faster then
Because there are no plants then
103005.e: In the morning the light is gentle and warm. Also, many animals are out and about then.
103005.m: Early in the morning the light for nature photos is nice and soft.

103006.q: What do you do if a bird gets nervous while you are photographing it?
103006.e: If an animal gets restless, you are too close. Then you calmly move away and leave it in peace.
103006.m: If an animal gets restless, move away slowly.

103007.q: What are very close-up photos of tiny things like insects called?
103007.e: For macro photos you take the picture from a short distance. That way you see small things very large.
103007.m: Macro photos show small things very large.

103008.q: Why don't you walk into a meadow full of flowers when taking photos?
a: Because the camera would get wet
Because the flowers would fly away
Because it is too dark there
103008.e: If you step into the meadow, you bend grass and flowers. So stay on the path.
103008.m: Stay on the path when taking photos.

a: Holding the camera steady or resting it on something
103009.e: If the camera moves when you press the button, the picture becomes blurry. A tripod or a stone to rest it on helps.
103009.m: Hold the camera steady so the photo comes out sharp.

103010.q: Why is it better not to use a flash with animals?
a: The bright flash frightens the animals
Because the flash breaks the camera
Because the animals become more colourful
103010.e: A sudden bright flash frightens animals. Nocturnal animals are especially disturbed by it.

103011.q: What is a hiding place for nature photographers?
103011.e: In a camouflage tent the animals can hardly see the photographer. That way they come closer and stay calm.
103011.m: In a camouflage tent the animals can hardly see the photographer.

103012.q: What do you call birds that fly away in autumn and come back in spring?
103012.e: Migratory birds travel back and forth every year between their summer and winter areas.
103012.m: Migratory birds fly away in autumn and come back in spring.

103013.q: What do you call birds that stay with us all year round?
103013.e: Resident birds stay in their area even in winter. One example is the house sparrow.
103013.m: Resident birds stay with us all year round.

103014.q: On which continent do many Swiss migratory birds spend the winter?
103014.e: Many migratory birds from Switzerland, such as the nightingale, spend the winter in Africa. It is warm there and there are insects.
103014.m: Many Swiss migratory birds spend the winter in Africa.

103015.q: In what shape do geese often fly across the sky?
103015.e: Geese and cranes often fly in a V shape. That way the birds behind use the air current of the ones in front and save energy.
103015.m: Geese often fly in a V shape to save energy.

103016.q: What do migratory birds do before their long journey?
a: They eat to build up fat
103016.e: The birds need lots of energy for the long flight. They store it beforehand as fat in their bodies.
103016.m: Before the journey migratory birds build up fat.

103017.q: Among other things, what do migratory birds use to find their way?
103017.e: Migratory birds find their way using the Sun, the stars and the Earth's magnetic field. Mountains and rivers also help them.
103017.m: Migratory birds find their way by the Sun and the stars.

103018.q: When do many small migratory birds fly?
103018.e: Many small songbirds migrate at night. During the day they rest and look for food.
103018.m: Many small migratory birds fly at night.

103019.q: Which bird flies the furthest on its migration, from the Arctic to the Antarctic?
103019.e: The Arctic tern breeds in the far north and flies all the way to the Antarctic in winter. No other bird migrates so far.
103019.m: The Arctic tern migrates further than any other bird.

103020.q: What does a bird get when it is ringed?
a: A small ring on its leg
103020.e: Scientists put a light ring around the bird's leg. That way it can be recognised later.
103020.m: When it is ringed, a bird gets a ring on its leg.

103021.q: What is written on a bird ring?
103021.e: Every ring has its own number and the address of a bird observatory. That way people know where the bird was ringed.
103021.m: Every bird ring has its own number.

a: To find out where they fly and how old they get
103022.e: If a ringed bird is found again, you know where it has been. That way you learn a lot about migration routes and age.
103022.m: Ringed birds reveal where they fly and how old they get.

103023.q: What do you do if you find a dead bird with a ring?
a: You report the ring number to the bird observatory
You keep the ring as jewellery
103023.e: The bird observatory is happy about every report. With the number it finds out where the bird came from.
103023.m: Report a bird ring you find to the bird observatory.

103024.q: What is the name of the well-known bird observatory in Switzerland?
103024.e: The Swiss Ornithological Institute is in Sempach in the canton of Lucerne. It studies and protects birds.
103024.m: The Swiss bird observatory is in Sempach.

103025.q: Who is allowed to ring birds?
a: Only trained experts with a permit
103025.e: Birds are delicate and must be held correctly. That is why only trained people with a permit may ring them.
103025.m: Only trained experts may ring birds.

103026.q: What do scientists use to catch small birds for ringing?
103026.e: Very fine nets, called mist nets, are used. The birds are carefully taken out, ringed and released again.
103026.m: Small birds are caught with fine nets for ringing.

103027.q: What happens to a bird right after it is ringed?
103027.e: After ringing, weighing and measuring, the bird flies free again. The ring doesn't bother it.
103027.m: After ringing, the bird is released again.

103028.q: What do scientists often measure as well when ringing?
a: The weight and the wing length
How many brothers and sisters it has
103028.e: The bird is weighed and its wings are measured. That shows whether it is healthy and well fed.
103028.m: When ringed, birds are also weighed and measured.

103029.q: What colour are the white stork's beak and legs?
103029.e: The white stork has a red beak and red legs. Its feathers are white with black wing feathers.
103029.m: The white stork has a red beak and red legs.

103030.q: Where does the white stork often build its nest?
103030.e: Storks like to build their big nests high up on roofs, chimneys or poles.
103030.m: Storks often build their nests on roofs and chimneys.

103031.q: How does a stork make sounds?
103031.e: Adult storks hardly have a voice. They clatter their beaks loudly, which is why in German the stork is also nicknamed “Klapperstorch”, the clattering stork.

103032.q: What does the white stork like to eat?
103032.e: The stork strides across meadows and catches frogs, mice, earthworms and insects.
103032.m: The stork eats frogs, mice and insects.

103033.q: What did people in Switzerland do when white storks had disappeared around 1950?
103033.e: From 1948, Max Bloesch brought storks to Switzerland in Altreu in the canton of Solothurn and helped them to breed again. Today there are lots of stork pairs again.
103033.m: White storks were brought back to Switzerland.

103034.q: Where do many Swiss storks fly in winter?
103034.e: Many storks migrate to Africa. Today some already stay in Spain, where they find food on rubbish tips.
103034.m: Many storks spend the winter in Spain or Africa.

103035.q: What colour are the big wing feathers of the white stork?
103035.e: The stork is almost completely white. Only the big feathers on the wings are black.
103035.m: The white stork's big wing feathers are black.

103036.q: What do storks often do with their old nest?
a: They use it again every year
They give it to the sparrows
103036.e: Storks often come back to the same nest and keep adding to it. Over the years it becomes very big and heavy.
103036.m: Storks often use their nest for many years.

103037.q: Why does a bird build a nest?
a: To lay eggs and raise its young in it
To sleep through the winter in it
103037.e: In the nest the eggs are warm and safe. Later the young birds grow up there.
103037.m: Birds lay eggs and raise their young in a nest.

103038.q: What do many birds use for their nest?
103038.e: Many birds weave twigs and grass together. Inside they line the nest with moss, hair or feathers.
103038.m: Many nests are made of twigs, grass and moss.

103039.q: Which bird carves its nest as a hole in a tree trunk?
103039.e: The woodpecker hacks a hole into the wood with its strong beak. It nests inside.
103039.m: The woodpecker carves a nesting hole in the tree.

103040.q: What can you hang up to help birds nest?
103040.e: In a nest box, tits and other birds that nest in holes find a safe place for their nest.
103040.m: A nest box helps birds to nest.

103041.q: When is the best time to clean a nest box?
a: In autumn, when no birds are nesting
When there are young in it
103041.e: In autumn the nesting season is over. Then you can remove the old nest without disturbing any birds.
103041.m: Nest boxes are cleaned in autumn.

103042.q: Which bird weaves skilful nests out of blades of grass?
103042.e: Weaver birds live mainly in Africa. They knot and weave nests out of blades of grass that hang from branches.
103042.m: Weaver birds weave their nests out of grass.

103043.q: Why shouldn't you touch a bird's nest?
a: The parents could be disturbed and leave the nest
Because it would then grow faster
103043.e: Disturbing the nest can drive the bird parents away. That is why you only look at nests from a distance.
103043.m: You only look at birds' nests from a distance.

103044.q: Where does the mallard often nest?
a: In a hollow on the ground
103044.e: The mallard usually builds its nest well hidden on the ground, often near water. It lines it with its own down.
103044.m: The mallard usually nests on the ground.

103045.q: In most bird species, who does most of the singing?
103045.e: In most songbirds it is mainly the males that sing. They use song to mark their territory and attract females.

103046.q: How do young songbirds learn their song?
a: They listen to the older birds
They already know it in the egg
103046.e: Young songbirds listen to the adults' song and copy it. At first it still sounds unfinished.
103046.m: Young birds learn their song by listening.

103047.q: Which bird is known for its beautiful song at night?
103047.e: The nightingale also sings at night. Its song is very varied and loud.
103047.m: The nightingale also sings at night.

103048.q: Which tiny brown bird sings amazingly loudly?
103048.e: The wren is one of the smallest birds in Switzerland. Even so, it sings very loudly.
103048.m: The little wren sings very loudly.

103049.q: What do you call it when lots of birds sing at the same time early on a spring morning?
103049.e: At dawn many birds start to sing one after another. Together it sounds like a big choir.
103049.m: On spring mornings lots of birds sing in the dawn chorus.

103050.q: In which season do most birds sing the most?
103050.e: In spring birds look for a territory and a partner. That is why they sing especially much then.
103050.m: Birds sing the most in spring.

103051.q: How do bird experts recognise a bird species even when they can't see it?
a: By the size of the tree
103051.e: Every bird species sings differently. Experts recognise many birds just by their song.
103051.m: You can recognise bird species by their song.

103052.q: What do scientists use to record bird calls?
103052.e: With a microphone and a recorder you can record birdsong and listen to it closely later.
103052.m: Bird calls are recorded with a microphone.

103053.e: Today only birds have feathers. Feathers are the most important feature of birds.

103054.q: What are the soft, fluffy feathers that keep a bird warm called?
103054.e: Down feathers are soft and loose. They hold a lot of air and keep the bird warm.

103055.q: Which feathers does a bird mainly need for flying?
a: The flight feathers on its wings
103055.e: The long, stiff flight feathers on the wings carry the bird through the air.
103055.m: A bird needs its flight feathers to fly.

103056.q: What do you call it when a bird loses its old feathers and grows new ones?
103056.e: When moulting, the bird changes its feathers bit by bit. That way worn-out feathers are replaced.
103056.m: When it moults, a bird gets new feathers.

103057.q: What are feathers made of, just like your fingernails?
103057.e: Feathers are made of a horny material called keratin. Hair and fingernails are made of it too.
103057.m: Feathers are made of horn, like your fingernails.

103058.q: Why do ducks stay dry in the water?
a: They only swim for a short time
Their feathers are made of metal
103058.e: Ducks have an oil gland at the base of their tail. They use it to oil their feathers, so the water runs off.
103058.m: Ducks oil their feathers to stay dry.

103059.q: What did people often use to write with in the past?
103059.e: In the past people cut the tip of a large goose feather into shape. Then they dipped it in ink and wrote with it.
103059.m: In the past people wrote with goose quills.

103060.q: Why are the feathers of many female birds rather brown and plain?
a: So they are well camouflaged when sitting on eggs
103060.e: When sitting on the eggs, the female stays on the nest for a long time. Brown feathers hide her from enemies.
103060.m: Brown feathers camouflage females sitting on eggs.

103061.q: What is a bird doing when it arranges and cleans its feathers with its beak?
103061.e: Birds pull each feather through their beak. That keeps the feathers clean, smooth and ready for flying.
103061.m: Birds clean their feathers with their beaks.

103062.q: What colour is the throat of the barn swallow?
103062.e: The barn swallow has a reddish-brown throat and forehead. Its back shines dark blue.
103062.m: The barn swallow has a reddish-brown throat.

103063.q: How can you recognise the barn swallow in flight?
a: By the long streamers on its tail
103063.e: The barn swallow has a deeply forked tail with two long streamers. That makes it easy to recognise.
103063.m: The barn swallow has long tail streamers.

103064.q: Where does the barn swallow usually build its nest?
103064.e: Barn swallows like to nest in cowsheds and barns. There they find shelter and lots of flies.
103064.m: Barn swallows like to nest in cowsheds.

103065.q: What does the barn swallow eat?
103065.e: The barn swallow catches flies and mosquitoes in flight. That is why it often flies low over meadows.
103065.m: Barn swallows catch insects in flight.

103066.q: Where does the barn swallow spend the winter?
103066.e: In winter there are no flying insects here. So the barn swallow flies all the way to Africa.
103066.m: The barn swallow spends the winter in Africa.

103067.q: Why do swallows often fly low before a thunderstorm?
a: Because they want to drink raindrops
Because they are scared of the thunder
103067.e: In damp, muggy air many insects fly closer to the ground. The swallows hunt them there.
103067.m: Swallows fly low when the insects fly low.

103068.q: What does an old saying say about a single swallow?
a: One swallow does not make a summer
103068.e: When the first swallow arrives, summer is not here yet. The saying means that one single sign is not enough.
103068.m: One swallow does not make a summer.

103069.q: Where does the golden eagle live in Switzerland?
a: On the shores of large lakes
In the forests of the Swiss Plateau
103069.e: The golden eagle lives in the mountains. It hunts over alpine pastures and nests on steep cliffs.
103069.m: The golden eagle lives in the Alps.

103070.q: Which mountain animal does the golden eagle often hunt in summer?
103070.e: Marmots are important prey for the golden eagle. They whistle loudly when they see an eagle.
103070.m: The golden eagle often hunts marmots.

103071.q: What is the big nest of an eagle called?
103071.e: The nest of a large bird of prey is called an eyrie. The golden eagle usually builds its eyrie on a cliff face.
103071.m: An eagle's nest is called an eyrie.

103072.q: Roughly how wide are the outstretched wings of a golden eagle?
103072.e: From one wingtip to the other, a golden eagle measures about 2 metres.
103072.m: A golden eagle has a wingspan of about 2 metres.

103073.q: What does the golden eagle use to grab its prey?
103073.e: The golden eagle has strong feet with sharp claws called talons. It grabs its prey with them.
103073.m: The golden eagle grabs its prey with its talons.

103074.q: What colour are the feathers of an adult golden eagle mainly?
103074.e: The golden eagle is dark brown. On the back of its head the feathers shimmer golden yellow.
103074.m: The golden eagle is dark brown with a golden neck.

103075.q: Why can the golden eagle see prey from high up?
a: It feels the prey with its feathers
103075.e: Eagles see much more sharply than people. They can spot a marmot from a great distance.

103077.q: What does the bearded vulture mainly eat?
103077.e: The bearded vulture mainly eats bones of dead animals. Its stomach acid is so strong that it can digest them.
103077.m: The bearded vulture mainly eats bones.

103078.q: How did the bearded vulture get its name?
a: From the black feathers under its beak
103078.e: Under its beak the bearded vulture has black bristly feathers. They look like a beard.
103078.m: The bearded vulture has feathers like a beard under its beak.

103079.q: What does the bearded vulture do with big bones?
a: It drops them on rocks until they break
It buries them in the snow
It throws them into the water
It builds its nest out of them
103079.e: The bearded vulture carries bones that are too big up into the air and drops them on rocks. That breaks them into pieces.
103079.m: Bearded vultures break bones by dropping them.

103080.q: Why is the bearded vulture's chest often orange?
103080.e: The chest feathers are actually white. The bearded vulture colours them itself by bathing in reddish mud.
103080.m: The bearded vulture colours its chest orange in mud.

103081.q: What happened to the bearded vulture in the Alps in the past?
103081.e: People wrongly believed that it stole lambs and children. So it was hunted until there were no bearded vultures left in the Alps.
103081.m: The bearded vulture was once wiped out in the Alps.

103082.q: In which Swiss area were the first bearded vultures released in 1991?
103082.e: In 1991 young bearded vultures were released into the wild in the National Park in the Engadine. Today bearded vultures breed in Switzerland again.
103082.m: In 1991 bearded vultures returned to Switzerland in the National Park.

103083.q: Is the bearded vulture dangerous to people?
a: No, it only eats dead animals
103083.e: The bearded vulture doesn't kill large animals and certainly not people. It feeds on dead animals.
103083.m: The bearded vulture is harmless to people.

103084.q: Roughly how big is the bearded vulture's wingspan?
103084.e: With a wingspan of almost 3 metres, the bearded vulture is one of the largest birds in the Alps.
103084.m: The bearded vulture has a wingspan of almost 3 metres.

103085.q: Where does the swift spend almost its whole life?
103085.e: The swift eats, drinks and even sleeps in flight. It only lands to nest.
103085.m: The swift spends almost its whole life in the air.

103086.q: Where does the swift often nest?
a: In cracks and holes in buildings
103086.e: Swifts nest in holes in walls, under roofs and in cracks in buildings. That is why in German they are called “wall sailors”.
103086.m: Swifts nest in holes in buildings.

103087.q: Why does a swift find it hard to take off from flat ground?
a: It has very short legs and long wings
It has very long legs and short wings
It is too heavy to take off
It has too few feathers on its wings
103087.e: With its short legs the swift can hardly push itself up, and its long wings hit the ground. It prefers to take off from high places.
103087.m: Swifts prefer to take off from high places rather than from the ground.

103088.q: What does the call of swifts over the town sound like?
103088.e: In summer swifts chase each other in groups over the rooftops. They call loudly and shrilly as they do.

a: As early as the start of August
103089.e: Swifts stay with us for only about three months. Most of them fly to Africa as early as the start of August.
103089.m: Swifts fly to Africa as early as the start of August.

103090.e: With its beak wide open, the swift catches tiny insects and spiders floating in the air.
103090.m: Swifts eat small insects from the air.

103091.q: How does a swift sleep during migration?
103091.e: Scientists found out that swifts rest in flight. They can stay in the air for months.

103092.q: What shape are the swift's wings?
103092.e: The swift's wings are long, narrow and curved like a sickle. With them it flies fast and for a long time.

103093.q: What is the hard shell of a bird's egg mainly made of?
103093.e: Eggshell is mainly made of lime. It protects the chick and still lets air through.
103093.m: Eggshell is mainly made of lime.

103094.q: Why do birds sit on their eggs?
103094.e: The eggs need warmth so the chick can grow. Sitting on the eggs is called brooding.
103094.m: Birds hatch their eggs with their body warmth.

103095.q: What shape are most birds' eggs?
a: Oval, more pointed at one end
103095.e: Most birds' eggs are oval and a bit more pointed at one end. A perfectly round or angular shape is very rare in birds' eggs.

103096.q: Roughly how long does a hen sit on her eggs until the chick hatches?
103096.e: A chick hatches after about three weeks. That is around 21 days.
103096.m: A chick hatches after about 21 days.

103097.q: What does a chick use to break open the eggshell?
a: A small egg tooth on its beak
103097.e: The chick has a small hard bump at the front of its beak called the egg tooth. It uses it to peck open the shell.
103097.m: The chick pecks open the shell with its egg tooth.

103098.q: Why do many birds' eggs have spots?
103098.e: Speckled eggs look like stones or soil. That makes it harder for enemies to find them.

103099.e: Blackbird eggs are pale blue-green with brownish spots.
103099.m: Blackbird eggs are blue-green with brown spots.

103100.q: What is the food for the chick inside a bird's egg?
103100.e: The yellow yolk contains lots of food. The chick feeds on it while it grows inside the egg.
103100.m: The yolk is the food for the chick in the egg.

103101.q: Which bird lays the smallest eggs?
103101.e: Hummingbirds are the smallest birds in the world. Their eggs are only about the size of a pea or a small bean.
103101.m: Hummingbirds lay the smallest birds' eggs.

103102.q: Where does the cuckoo lay its eggs?
a: In the sand by the lake
In a hole in the ground
103102.e: The cuckoo doesn't build its own nest. The female lays her eggs in the nests of other kinds of birds.
103102.m: The cuckoo lays its eggs in other birds' nests.

103103.e: The host parents don't notice the trick. They feed the young cuckoo as if it were their own chick.
103103.m: Other bird parents raise the young cuckoo.

103104.q: What does the young cuckoo do soon after hatching?
a: It pushes the other eggs out of the nest
103104.e: The young cuckoo pushes the other eggs or chicks out of the nest. That way it gets all the food for itself.
103104.m: The young cuckoo pushes the other eggs out of the nest.

103105.q: What does the cuckoo like to eat that other birds avoid?
103105.e: Many birds don't like hairy caterpillars. The cuckoo likes eating them.
103105.m: The cuckoo likes eating hairy caterpillars.

103106.q: Where does the cuckoo spend the winter?
103106.e: The cuckoo is a migratory bird. It spends the winter in Africa south of the Sahara.
103106.m: The cuckoo spends the winter in Africa.

103107.q: Why is the young cuckoo soon much bigger than its foster parents?
a: The cuckoo is a bigger kind of bird
It stays in the egg longer
It sleeps more than other chicks
103107.e: The cuckoo is a large kind of bird. So the young one grows much bigger than the small foster parents feeding it.
103107.m: The young cuckoo grows bigger than its foster parents.

103108.q: Which area does the famous cuckoo clock come from?
103108.e: The cuckoo clock became famous in the Black Forest in Germany. A little wooden bird calls out on the hour.
103108.m: The cuckoo clock comes from the Black Forest.

103109.q: When can you hear the cuckoo calling here?
103109.e: The cuckoo comes back from Africa in April. You can hear its call until early summer.
103109.m: You hear the cuckoo in spring and early summer.

103110.q: What do you call tiny living things and particles that can make us ill?
103110.e: Germs, or pathogens, can get into the body through the mouth, nose or small wounds. There they multiply and make us ill.
103110.m: Germs are tiny and can make us ill.

103111.q: Can you see germs with the naked eye?
103111.e: Most germs are much smaller than a grain of sand. You need a microscope to see them.

103112.q: How long should you rub your hands with soap?
103112.e: The soap needs some time to loosen dirt and germs. You also rub between your fingers and under your nails.
103112.m: Thorough handwashing takes at least 20 seconds.

103113.q: Which kinds of germs are there, for example?
103113.e: Pathogens are mainly bacteria, viruses and some fungi. Some worms can also make you ill.
103113.m: Bacteria, viruses and fungi can cause illnesses.

103114.q: Where in the kitchen do especially many germs often live?
103114.e: A washing-up sponge is damp, warm and full of food scraps. Bacteria multiply very well there, so you change it often.
103114.m: You should change a washing-up sponge often.

103115.q: Why don’t you cut raw meat and salad on the same board?
a: Germs can get onto the salad
103115.e: There can be germs on raw meat. The salad is not cooked, so these germs would not be killed.
103115.m: Use a separate chopping board for raw meat.

103116.e: After the toilet there can be germs from the gut on your hands. Soap washes them away.
103116.m: Always wash your hands after the toilet.

103117.q: What helps the body defend itself well against germs?
a: Watching TV for a long time
103117.e: If you sleep well, move and eat healthily, you strengthen your defences. Then your body can fight germs better.
103117.m: Sleep and healthy food strengthen your defences.

103118.q: Which common illness with a runny nose, sore throat and cough is usually caused by viruses?
103118.e: A cold is usually caused by viruses, for example rhinoviruses. It is usually over after about a week.
103118.m: A cold usually comes from viruses.

103119.q: Which illness is caused by a virus?
103119.e: Real flu is caused by the influenza virus. Tooth decay, on the other hand, is caused by bacteria in the mouth.

103120.q: Can you see viruses with the naked eye?
a: No, they are far too small
Yes, they are as big as grains of sand
103120.e: Viruses are tiny, much smaller than a grain of sand. You can only see them with very special microscopes.
103120.m: Viruses are far too small to see.

103121.q: Which illness did the coronavirus cause around the world from 2020?
103121.e: A new coronavirus spread worldwide from early 2020. The illness it causes is called Covid-19.
103121.m: Covid-19 is caused by a coronavirus.

103122.e: Chickenpox is caused by the varicella-zoster virus. Itchy blisters all over the body are typical.

103123.q: Why can you catch flu again and again?
a: Flu only comes from the weather
103123.e: Flu viruses keep changing a little. That is why the body’s defences don’t always recognise them again.

103124.q: What often grows on old bread as green or white fluff?
103124.e: Mould often grows on old, damp bread. It looks like a fluffy coating.
103124.m: Fluff on old bread is usually mould.

103125.q: What does mould especially need to grow?
103125.e: Moulds grow best where it is damp and warm. In the fridge they grow more slowly.
103125.m: Mould likes it damp and warm.

103126.q: What do you do with a mouldy loaf of bread?
103126.e: The fine threads of mould often grow invisibly deep into the bread. That is why you throw the whole loaf away.
103126.m: Mouldy bread belongs entirely in the bin.

a: Through tiny spores in the air
103127.e: Moulds form tiny spores. These fly through the air and grow wherever it is damp.
103127.m: Mould spreads through the air with spores.

103128.q: Which medicine was obtained from a mould?
103128.e: In 1928 Alexander Fleming discovered that a mould kills bacteria. Penicillin was made from it.

103129.q: Which cheese deliberately has a white mould on the outside?
103129.e: On Camembert, an edible white mould grows on the rind. It gives the cheese its flavour.
103129.m: Camembert has an edible white mould.

103130.q: What helps against mould on the walls of a flat?
103130.e: When you air the rooms, damp air goes out. Without much damp, mould can hardly grow on the walls.

103131.q: Which group of living things does mould belong to?
103131.e: Mould is a fungus. It is made of fine threads and forms spores.

103132.q: Why shouldn’t you sniff mouldy food?
103132.e: When you sniff, mould spores get into your nose and lungs. That can be unhealthy and trigger allergies.

103134.q: What does the body learn from a vaccination?
103134.e: A vaccination shows the body a harmless part of a germ. That way the defences learn to recognise and fight the real germ quickly.
103134.m: A vaccination trains the body’s defences.

103135.q: Where are a child’s vaccinations recorded?
103135.e: The vaccination record shows which vaccinations you had and when. That way the doctor knows what is still missing.
103135.m: The vaccination record shows all vaccinations.

103136.q: What do you call a vaccination that strengthens protection again after a few years?
103136.e: With some vaccinations, for example against tetanus, the protection fades over time. A booster makes it strong again.
103136.m: A booster strengthens vaccine protection again.

103137.q: Which disease no longer exists in the world thanks to vaccinations?
103137.e: Smallpox was defeated with worldwide vaccinations. In 1980 the World Health Organization declared it wiped out.
103137.m: Smallpox was wiped out thanks to vaccinations.

103138.q: Which three diseases does the MMR vaccine protect against?
103138.e: The MMR vaccine is a triple vaccine. The three letters stand for the first letters of the three childhood diseases.
103138.m: The MMR vaccine protects against three childhood diseases.

103139.q: Which disease from tick bites can you be vaccinated against?
103139.e: TBE is an inflammation of the brain and its lining that is passed on by ticks. This vaccination is recommended in large parts of Switzerland.
103139.m: There is a vaccine against the tick disease TBE.

103140.q: What can happen for a short time after a vaccination?
103140.e: The injection spot can be a bit red or sore for one or two days. Sometimes you also get a slight temperature.
103140.m: After a vaccination your arm can hurt for a short time.

103141.q: Which disease, also known as polio, are children vaccinated against today?
103141.e: Infantile paralysis, also called polio, is caused by a virus and can paralyse muscles. Thanks to vaccinations it hardly occurs in Europe any more.

103142.q: How does a vaccination also protect other people?
103142.e: If you are vaccinated, you get ill less often and pass on germs less often. That way babies and sick people are also better protected.
103142.m: Vaccination also protects the people around us.

103143.e: Measles is caused by the measles virus. It gets into the body when you breathe.
103143.m: Measles is caused by a virus.

103144.q: What do you see on the skin with measles?
103144.e: After a few days you get red spots that often start behind the ears and on the face. Then they spread over the whole body.

103145.e: Measles is one of the most contagious diseases of all. Almost every unprotected person who comes into contact with the virus becomes ill.

103146.q: How is the measles virus usually passed on?
103146.e: When people cough, sneeze or talk, tiny droplets with the virus get into the air. Anyone who breathes them in can be infected.

103147.q: Which symptoms do you often have at the start of measles?
103147.e: Measles starts like a bad cold with fever, a runny nose and a cough. The eyes are often red too.
103147.m: Measles starts with fever and a cough.

103148.q: How many times in your life do you usually get measles?
103148.e: Anyone who has had measles is usually protected for life afterwards. The body remembers the virus.
103148.m: After measles you are usually protected for good.

103149.q: How many doses of measles vaccine does the Swiss vaccination plan recommend?
103149.e: For safe protection you need two vaccinations. In Switzerland, young children get them in their first and second year of life.
103149.m: For protection against measles you need two vaccinations.

a: Yes, it only lasts an hour
Yes, you don’t notice it at all
103150.e: Measles can lead to pneumonia or inflammation of the brain. That is why protection through vaccination is important.

103151.q: What does a child with mumps often look like?
a: With red spots all over the body
103151.e: With mumps, the salivary glands in front of the ears swell up. The face then looks like a hamster with full cheeks.

103152.q: Which gland swells up with mumps?
103152.e: The parotid gland is in front of and below the ear. It makes saliva and becomes swollen and painful with mumps.
103152.m: With mumps, the parotid gland swells up.

103154.e: The mumps virus is in saliva. It can be passed on by coughing, sneezing, a kiss on the cheek or sharing a glass.
103154.m: Mumps is passed on through saliva.

103155.q: Besides swollen cheeks, what else do you often have with mumps?
103155.e: Many children with mumps have a fever and a headache and feel weak. Chewing can hurt too.
103155.m: Mumps often comes with fever and a headache.

103156.q: How common is mumps in Switzerland today compared with the past?
103156.e: Since there has been a vaccine, far fewer children catch mumps. In the past almost every child got this illness.
103156.m: Thanks to vaccination, mumps has become rare.

103157.q: What should a child with mumps do?
103157.e: Mumps is contagious. If you are ill, you rest at home so you don’t infect anyone.
103157.m: With mumps you stay at home.

103158.e: Mumps is caused by the mumps virus and passes from person to person. It is a typical childhood illness.
103158.m: Mumps is a contagious viral illness.

103159.q: What do you see on the skin with rubella?
103159.e: With rubella, small light red spots appear on the skin. They usually only itch a little.

103160.q: Where does the rubella rash usually start?
103160.e: The rash usually starts on the face and behind the ears. Then it spreads over the body.
103160.m: The rubella rash starts on the face.

103161.q: What often swells up with rubella?
a: The lymph nodes in the neck
103161.e: With rubella, the lymph nodes in the neck and behind the ears get swollen. They are part of the body’s defences.
103161.m: With rubella, the lymph nodes in the neck swell up.

103162.q: How serious is rubella in children usually?
103162.e: In children, rubella is usually a mild illness. Many only have a slight fever and a rash.
103162.m: Rubella is usually mild in children.

103164.e: Rubella is caused by the rubella virus. It is passed on by coughing and talking.
103164.m: Rubella is caused by a virus.

103165.q: How long does the rubella rash usually last?
103165.e: The rubella rash usually disappears after one to three days. It leaves no scars.
103165.m: The rubella rash disappears after a few days.

103166.q: Does every child notice when they have rubella?
103166.e: Many rubella infections pass without clear signs. You can still pass the virus on.
103166.m: You can have rubella without noticing.

103167.e: Whooping cough is caused by the bacterium Bordetella pertussis. It settles in the airways.
103167.m: Whooping cough is caused by bacteria.

103168.q: What is typical of whooping cough?
103168.e: With whooping cough you get violent coughing fits. You cough many times in a row.
103168.m: Whooping cough causes strong coughing fits.

103169.q: What sound do you hear after a coughing fit with whooping cough?
a: A drawn-out gasp when breathing in
A loud whistle when breathing out
103169.e: After the coughing fit, you draw in air with a gasping, whooping sound. That is where the illness gets its name.
103169.m: With whooping cough you gasp in air after coughing.

103170.q: How long does whooping cough often last?
103170.e: The cough with whooping cough can last many weeks. In China it is even called the “hundred-day cough”.
103170.m: Whooping cough often lasts many weeks.

103171.q: Who is whooping cough especially dangerous for?
103171.e: Babies with whooping cough can stop breathing for short moments. That is why the people around them should protect themselves too.
103171.m: Whooping cough is especially dangerous for babies.

103172.q: How is whooping cough passed on?
103172.e: When people cough and sneeze, tiny droplets with the bacteria fly through the air. Others breathe them in.

103173.e: There is a vaccine against whooping cough. The Swiss vaccination plan recommends it for babies already.
103173.m: A vaccination protects against whooping cough.

103174.q: When do the coughing fits of whooping cough often come especially often?
103174.e: With whooping cough, the coughing fits are often especially strong at night. That is why sick children sleep badly.

103175.q: Which parts of a microscope make the image bigger?
103175.e: A microscope contains several glass lenses. They bend the light so that small things look big.
103175.m: Glass lenses in the microscope make the image bigger.

103176.q: What is the small glass plate called that you put the sample on for a microscope?
103176.e: The sample goes on a thin glass slide. Often a cover slip is placed on top.
103176.m: The sample lies on a slide.

103177.q: What is the part of the microscope you look into called?
103177.e: The eyepiece is the lens you hold your eye to. Its technical name, ocular, comes from the Latin “oculus”, eye.
103177.m: You look into the microscope through the eyepiece.

103178.q: Who was one of the first people to see bacteria, around 1676, with a microscope he built himself?
103178.e: The Dutchman Antonie van Leeuwenhoek made tiny, very powerful lenses. With them he discovered small living things that he called “little animals”.
103178.m: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek discovered bacteria with the microscope.

103179.q: Which device magnifies less than a microscope?
103179.e: A magnifying glass is a single lens and only magnifies a few times. A microscope magnifies much more.
103179.m: A magnifying glass magnifies less than a microscope.

103180.q: The eyepiece magnifies 10 times and the objective lens also 10 times. How much does the microscope magnify?
103180.e: You multiply the two magnifications: 10 times 10 makes 100. So the image is 100 times bigger.
103180.m: The magnifications of eyepiece and objective are multiplied.

103181.q: Where does the light usually come from on a school microscope?
a: From above out of the eyepiece
From the side through the window
103181.e: There is a lamp under the stage of the microscope. Its light shines up through the thin sample into your eye.
103181.m: On a school microscope, light shines from below through the sample.

103182.q: What do you see under the microscope in a drop of pond water?
103182.e: Countless tiny living things such as slipper animalcules and algae live in pond water. With a microscope you can see them swimming around.
103182.m: Tiny living things live in a drop of pond water.

103183.q: What do you use to bring the image into focus on a microscope?
103183.e: There are focus knobs on the stand of the microscope. When you turn them, the stage moves until the image is sharp.
103183.m: You focus the image with the focus knob.

103185.q: Which illness do you often catch when someone coughs on you?
103185.e: When someone coughs, tiny droplets with germs fly through the air. Anyone who breathes them in can catch a cold.
103185.m: Cold germs fly through the air when people cough.

103186.q: What do you call infection through hands and objects?
103186.e: Germs can sit on door handles, toys and hands. If you then touch your mouth, nose or eyes, you become infected.
103186.m: You can also be infected through hands and objects.

103188.q: Why is it better not to touch your eyes, nose and mouth often?
a: Germs get into the body that way
103188.e: There are often germs on your hands. They can easily get into the body through the eyes, nose and mouth.
103188.m: Don’t touch your face with unwashed hands.

103189.q: What does it mean if an illness is contagious?
a: It can pass to other people
It only lasts a short time
103189.e: A contagious illness is caused by germs. These can travel from one person to the next.
103189.m: Contagious illnesses pass to other people.

103190.q: Which of these complaints is not contagious?
103190.e: Sunburn is caused by too much sun on the skin. It is not caused by germs and cannot be passed on.

103191.q: Why don’t you drink from the same bottle as a friend who is ill?
103191.e: Saliva with germs stays on the neck of the bottle. Whoever drinks next can be infected.
103191.m: Don’t share a drinking bottle with someone who is ill.

103192.e: Hay fever is an allergy and is not caused by germs. That is why you cannot infect anyone with it.

103193.q: When do many people have hay fever?
103193.e: In spring and summer, trees, grasses and herbs flower. Then especially large amounts of pollen fly through the air.
103193.m: Hay fever comes mainly in spring and summer.

103194.q: The pollen of which tree often causes hay fever in Switzerland?
103194.e: Birch pollen is one of the most common causes of hay fever. Birch trees usually flower in April.
103194.m: Birch pollen often causes hay fever.

103195.q: What often happens to your eyes with hay fever?
103195.e: The pollen irritates the eyes. The defences react, and the eyes go red, itch and water.
103195.m: With hay fever your eyes often itch.

103196.q: What happens in the body with an allergy?
103196.e: With an allergy, the defences think harmless substances such as pollen are dangerous. They fight back too strongly.
103196.m: With an allergy, the defences react too strongly.

103197.q: Which shrub flowers in winter and can cause hay fever early?
103197.e: Hazel often flowers as early as January or February. Its yellow catkins then release lots of pollen.

103198.q: What helps with hay fever in the evening?
103198.e: During the day lots of pollen gets caught in your hair. If you wash it in the evening, less pollen gets into your bed.
103198.m: Washing your hair in the evening keeps pollen out of bed.

103199.q: Who publishes pollen forecasts in Switzerland?
103199.e: MeteoSwiss measures in many places how much pollen is in the air. That way people with allergies can prepare for high pollen counts.

103200.q: What forms in the mouth with hand, foot and mouth disease?
103200.e: Small blisters that can hurt appear in the mouth. There are also spots and blisters on the hands and feet.
103200.m: With this illness you have blisters in your mouth.

103201.q: What causes hand, foot and mouth disease?
103201.e: The illness is caused by certain viruses called enteroviruses. It passes from person to person.
103201.m: Hand, foot and mouth disease is caused by viruses.

103202.q: Who gets hand, foot and mouth disease most often?
103202.e: Mainly children under ten catch it, often at nursery and kindergarten. Adults are usually already protected.
103202.m: Mainly young children get hand, foot and mouth disease.

103203.q: How does hand, foot and mouth disease usually go?
a: Harmlessly, better after about a week
Always with a stay in hospital
103203.e: The illness usually heals by itself after seven to ten days. Serious cases are rare.
103203.m: Hand, foot and mouth disease usually heals by itself.

103204.q: Why do children with hand, foot and mouth disease often eat badly?
a: The blisters in the mouth hurt
103204.e: The blisters in the mouth hurt when chewing and swallowing. Cool, soft food and lots to drink help.
103204.m: Cool, soft food helps with blisters in the mouth.

103205.q: What protects well against hand, foot and mouth disease?
103205.e: The viruses are in saliva, in the blisters and in poo. Frequent handwashing stops them being passed on.
103205.m: Handwashing protects against hand, foot and mouth disease.

103206.q: Where do you get spots and blisters with hand, foot and mouth disease?
a: On the hands, feet and in the mouth
103206.e: The name gives it away: the spots and blisters appear on the hands, on the feet and in the mouth.
103206.m: The blisters appear on the hands, feet and in the mouth.

103207.q: How does hand, foot and mouth disease often start?
a: With a fever and a sore throat
103207.e: At first you often have a slight fever, a sore throat and little appetite. One or two days later the blisters come.
103207.m: Hand, foot and mouth disease often starts with a fever.

103208.q: What are the points round the edge of a gear wheel called?
103208.e: Round the edge of a gear wheel there are lots of teeth of the same size. They fit into the teeth of another gear wheel.
103208.m: A gear wheel has teeth round its edge.

103209.q: Two gear wheels fit into each other. One turns to the right. Which way does the other turn?
103209.e: When two gear wheels fit into each other, they always turn in opposite directions. The teeth push each other along.
103209.m: Two gear wheels side by side turn in opposite directions.

103210.q: A big gear wheel and a small one fit into each other. Which turns faster?
103210.e: The small gear wheel has fewer teeth. That is why it has to turn more often while the big one goes round once.
103210.m: The smaller gear wheel turns faster.

103211.q: One gear wheel has 20 teeth, another has 10 teeth. How many times does the small one turn when the big one turns once?
103211.e: In one turn of the big wheel, 20 teeth go past. The small wheel has 10 teeth, so it turns 20 divided by 10, which is 2 times.
103211.m: The fewer teeth the small wheel has, the more often it turns.

103212.q: On which vehicle do gear wheels with a chain drive the back wheel?
103212.e: On a bicycle you turn the front gear wheel with the pedals. The chain passes the movement on to a gear wheel on the back wheel.
103212.m: On a bicycle, a chain drives the back wheel.

103213.q: You turn the handle of a salad spinner. What do the gear wheels inside do?
103213.e: In a salad spinner a big gear wheel drives a small one. That way the basket turns much faster than the handle.
103213.m: Gear wheels can make turning faster.

103214.q: What are gear wheels in machines usually made of?
103214.e: Gear wheels have to be strong and hard so that the teeth don't break off. That is why they are usually made of metal or hard plastic.
103214.m: Gear wheels are usually made of metal or plastic.

103215.q: On a bike with gears, what do you do on a steep climb?
103215.e: In a low gear the chain sits on a big back gear wheel. That way you need less force, but you pedal more often.
103215.m: Uphill you change into a low gear.

103216.q: What drives the hands in a mechanical clock?
103216.e: Inside a mechanical clock there is a clockwork. Lots of small gear wheels move the hands on steadily.
103216.m: A clockwork moves the hands with gear wheels.

103217.q: What swings back and forth in a grandfather clock?
103217.e: The pendulum always swings back and forth at the same speed. That is how it makes sure the clock runs evenly.
103217.m: The pendulum makes a grandfather clock accurate.

103218.q: What do you have to do to an old clock without a battery to keep it running?
103218.e: Old clocks have a spring inside. When you wind it up, you tighten the spring. The spring then drives the clockwork.
103218.m: An old clock without a battery has to be wound up.

103219.q: What is the job of people who build and repair clockworks called?
103219.e: Watchmakers put tiny parts together to make clockworks. In Switzerland it is a well-known trade that you learn through an apprenticeship.

103220.q: Which clock has a bird that calls out every hour?
103220.e: On a cuckoo clock a little door opens on the hour. A small wooden bird comes out and calls “cuckoo”.
103220.m: On a cuckoo clock a wooden bird calls out the hours.

103221.q: What gives a battery clock its exact beat?
103221.e: In a quartz clock a tiny quartz crystal vibrates very fast and very evenly. The battery supplies the electricity for it.
103221.m: A quartz clock runs with a vibrating crystal.

103222.q: How does an automatic watch on your wrist wind itself up?
a: Through the movement of your arm
103222.e: In an automatic watch a weight turns when you move your arm. As it does, it tightens the spring in the clockwork.
103222.m: An automatic watch winds itself through movement.

103223.q: What do you hear if you hold a mechanical clock close to your ear?
103223.e: In the clockwork, small parts always move to the same beat. You hear that as a quiet ticking.

103225.q: What does the car of a lift hang from?
103225.e: The car hangs from strong steel cables. At the top, a motor pulls the cables over a pulley.
103225.m: A lift hangs from strong steel cables.

103226.q: What hangs on the other end of a lift's cables?
103226.e: The counterweight moves down when the car goes up. That way the motor needs much less force.
103226.m: A counterweight saves force in a lift.

103227.q: What does a sign in a lift show, for example?
a: How many people may ride in it
103227.e: Every lift may only carry a certain weight. That is why the car says how many people or kilograms are allowed.
103227.m: A lift shows how many people may ride in it.

103228.q: What should you not use if there is a fire in the building?
103228.e: In a fire the lift can get stuck or fill with smoke. That is why you always take the stairs.
103228.m: In a fire you take the stairs, not the lift.

103229.q: Who invented a brake that stops the lift if the cable breaks?
103229.e: The American Elisha Otis showed his safety brake around 1854. After that, passenger lifts were seen as safe.

103230.q: On which mountain by Lake Lucerne is the highest outdoor lift in Europe?
103230.e: The Hammetschwand Lift on the Bürgenstock has been going up a rock face since 1905. It is said to be the highest outdoor lift in Europe.
103230.m: The highest outdoor lift in Europe is on the Bürgenstock.

103231.e: On an escalator the steps go round in a loop like a belt. At the top they disappear and at the bottom they come out again.
103231.m: On an escalator the steps move.

103232.q: What do you hold on to on an escalator?
103232.e: The handrail moves at the same speed as the steps. If you hold on, you stand more safely.
103232.m: On an escalator you hold on to the handrail.

103233.q: On which side do people usually stand on an escalator in Switzerland?
103233.e: You stand on the right so that people in a hurry can walk past on the left. That is usual in many stations.
103233.m: On an escalator you stand on the right.

103234.q: Why shouldn't you stand on the yellow edges of an escalator?
103234.e: The yellow edges show the gap between the step and the side wall. Shoes or clothes can get caught there.
103234.m: On an escalator you don't stand on the yellow edge.

103235.q: What do you call a flat moving belt without steps, for example at an airport?
103235.e: A moving walkway is like an escalator, but flat and without steps. You often find one at airports with long walks.
103235.m: A moving walkway is a flat moving belt.

103236.q: How do you get safely to another floor with a pushchair?
103236.e: On an escalator a pushchair can tip over or get stuck. That is why it is better to take the lift.
103236.m: With a pushchair you take the lift.

103237.q: What happens to the steps at the top end of the escalator?
103237.e: At the top the steps slide flat together and disappear under a comb plate. Underneath they travel back down.
103237.m: The steps of an escalator go round in a loop.

103238.q: Where do you often find escalators?
103238.e: Escalators move lots of people quickly from one floor to another. That is why they are found where many people are on the move.
103238.m: Escalators are found where many people are on the move.

103239.q: What is a crane needed for on a building site?
103239.e: A crane lifts heavy things such as steel girders, bricks and concrete parts up high. That way they get to where the building work is happening.

103240.q: What is the tall crane you see on many building sites called?
103240.e: A tower crane has a tall tower and a long jib. The jib can turn round in a circle.
103240.m: Building sites often have a tower crane.

103241.q: What are the heavy concrete blocks at the back of a building crane for?
a: So the crane doesn't tip over
So birds can sit on them
103241.e: The concrete blocks are a counterweight. They balance the weight of the load at the front so that the crane stays in balance.
103241.m: A counterweight keeps the crane in balance.

103242.q: What is the load fixed to on a crane?
103242.e: A strong crane hook hangs at the end of the cable. The load is fixed to it with chains or straps.
103242.m: The load hangs on the crane hook.

103243.q: Where does the person who controls a tower crane often sit?
a: In a cab at the top of the crane
On the roof of a car
103243.e: The crane operator often sits high up in a small cab. Today many crane operators also control the crane with a remote control from the ground.
103243.m: The crane operator often sits high up in the cab.

103244.e: A mobile crane sits on a vehicle with lots of wheels. It can drive quickly to a building site and work there.
103244.m: A mobile crane drives to the building site on wheels.

103245.q: Why must you never stand under a load on a crane?
103245.e: A load can come loose or swing. That is why the area under the crane is closed to people on foot.
103245.m: Never stand under a hanging load.

103246.q: What does a digger dig with?
103246.e: At the end of the digger's arm there is a big bucket with teeth. The digger uses it to dig out soil and stones.
103246.m: A digger digs with a bucket.

103247.q: What do big diggers often move on so that they don't sink into the mud?
103247.e: Caterpillar tracks spread the digger's heavy weight over a large area. That way it sinks less into soft ground.
103247.m: Caterpillar tracks stop a digger sinking in.

103248.q: What moves a digger's arm with great force?
103248.e: A digger works with hydraulics. A pump presses oil into cylinders, and these push the arm with great force.
103248.m: A digger moves its arm with hydraulics.

103249.q: What is the small digger with legs that was invented in Switzerland for steep slopes called?
103249.e: A walking excavator can climb over steep ground with its legs. The Swiss Ernst Menzi developed it in the 1960s.
103249.m: The walking excavator is a Swiss invention.

103250.q: Where does the person who controls the digger sit?
103250.e: The digger driver sits in a cab and controls it with levers. The cab can turn with the top part of the digger.
103250.m: A digger is controlled from the cab.

103251.q: On many diggers, what can turn all the way round?
a: The top part with the cab
103251.e: On many diggers the whole top part with the cab and the arm can turn. That way the digger can dig and tip the soil to one side.
103251.m: The top part of a digger can turn.

103252.q: What does a digger often do with the soil it has dug out?
a: It loads it onto a lorry
It throws it into the air
103252.e: The digger tips the soil into the back of a lorry. The lorry then takes it away.
103252.m: A digger loads soil onto lorries.

103253.q: Which tool can be fitted to a digger instead of the bucket to smash concrete?
103253.e: A digger can carry different tools. With a breaker hammer it smashes concrete and rock.
103253.m: A digger can carry different tools.

103254.q: What do the cabins of an aerial cableway hang from?
103254.e: On an aerial cableway the cabins hang from strong steel cables. The cables are stretched between stations and pylons.
103254.m: The cabins of an aerial cableway hang from cables.

103255.q: What is the cable railway whose cars run on rails up the slope called?
103255.e: On a funicular the cars run on rails. A cable pulls them up the steep slope.
103255.m: A funicular runs on rails and is pulled by a cable.

103256.q: Which funicular in Switzerland is said to be the steepest in the world?
103256.e: Since 2017 the Stoos funicular in the canton of Schwyz has climbed gradients of up to 110 percent. Its cabins turn so that the floor stays level.
103256.m: The Stoos funicular is the steepest funicular in the world.

103257.q: On which kind of cable car do you sit on open seats?
103257.e: On a chairlift you sit on open chairs with a safety bar. In winter lots of skiers ride on them.
103257.m: On a chairlift you sit in the open air.

103258.q: What is special about the cabin of the Titlis Rotair?
103258.e: The cabin of the Rotair cable car up the Titlis turns all the way round once during the ride. That way all the passengers see the whole view.
103258.m: The cabin of the Titlis Rotair turns.

103259.q: What do many cable cars between the valley and the mountain have so that the cable doesn't hang too low?
103259.e: Tall steel pylons hold up the cable along the way. That way it doesn't hang down too far.
103259.m: Pylons hold up the cable of a cable car.

103260.q: What pulls the cable of a cable car?
a: A big motor in the station
103260.e: In one station a strong electric motor turns a large wheel. The cable runs over it and moves the cabins.
103260.m: A motor in the station moves the cable.

103261.q: Why do some mountain railways have a cogwheel under the carriage?
a: So they don't slip on steep slopes
103261.e: Smooth wheels would spin on steep rails. The cogwheel grips a toothed rack and pulls the train safely up.
103261.m: A rack railway doesn't slip on a steep slope.

103262.q: Which rack railway is said to be the steepest in the world?
103262.e: The Pilatus Railway runs from Alpnachstad up Mount Pilatus. It has a gradient of up to 48 percent.
103262.m: The Pilatus Railway is the steepest rack railway in the world.

103263.q: Which mountain has Europe's first rack railway run up since 1871?
103263.e: The Vitznau-Rigi Railway opened in 1871. It was the first mountain railway in Europe with a cogwheel.
103263.m: Europe's first rack railway runs up the Rigi.

103264.q: Which rack railway runs from Zermatt with a view of the Matterhorn?
103264.e: The Gornergrat Railway runs from Zermatt up to over 3000 metres. On the way you can see the Matterhorn.
103264.m: The Gornergrat Railway runs from Zermatt up to the Gornergrat.

103265.q: Which rack railway in the Bernese Oberland still often runs with steam locomotives today?
103265.e: The Brienz Rothorn Railway runs from Brienz up the Rothorn. Many of its locomotives are still powered by steam.
103265.m: A steam rack railway runs up the Brienzer Rothorn.

103266.q: Which station does the highest rack railway in Switzerland go to?
103266.e: The Jungfrau Railway runs through a tunnel in the Eiger and Mönch up to the Jungfraujoch. The station is at 3454 metres and is the highest in Europe.
103266.m: The Jungfraujoch is the highest railway station in Europe.

103267.q: Why do rack railways usually go slowly?
a: Because they run on very steep lines
Because they are made of wood
103267.e: Steep lines need a lot of power, and the cogwheel has to grip the rack safely. That is why rack railways travel at a gentle pace.
103267.m: Rack railways go slowly because the line is steep.

103268.q: Which rack railway runs from Lauterbrunnen and Grindelwald up to Kleine Scheidegg?
103268.e: The Wengernalp Railway runs from Lauterbrunnen via Wengen to Kleine Scheidegg and from there down to Grindelwald. At Kleine Scheidegg you change to the Jungfrau Railway.
103268.m: The Wengernalp Railway runs to Kleine Scheidegg.

103269.q: How many sails does a typical old windmill have?
103269.e: Most old windmills in Europe have four large sails. They are arranged in the shape of a cross.
103269.m: A typical old windmill has four sails.

103270.q: Which country has especially many old windmills?
103270.e: In the flat Netherlands there is often a lot of wind. Over a thousand old windmills still stand there today.
103270.m: The Netherlands are known for their windmills.

103271.q: Apart from grinding, what were many windmills in the Netherlands used for?
103271.e: Many parts of the Netherlands lie below sea level. Windmills pumped the water from the fields into canals.
103271.m: In the Netherlands, windmills pumped water away.

103272.q: What is made in a mill when grain is ground?
103272.e: The millstones grind the grains of corn into a fine powder. This powder is flour.

103273.q: What grinds the grains in an old mill?
103273.e: One millstone turns above another millstone that stays still. The grains are ground between them.

103274.q: What is the person who works in a mill called?
103274.e: The miller grinds the grain in the mill. That is where the common surname Miller comes from, and in German the very common surname Müller.
103274.m: The surname Miller comes from the job in the mill.

103275.q: What does a windmill have to do when the wind comes from a different direction?
a: Turn its sails into the wind
103275.e: The sails need the wind from the front. That is why on many windmills you can turn the roof with the sails.
103275.m: The sails of a windmill must face the wind.

103276.e: The flowing water of a stream turns a big water wheel. This drives the mill.
103276.m: A water wheel drives the watermill.

103277.q: What do you call a water wheel where the water falls onto the wheel from above?
103277.e: On an overshot water wheel the water flows into small buckets at the top. The weight of the water turns the wheel.
103277.m: On an overshot water wheel the water falls onto the wheel from above.

103278.q: What was done in a sawmill powered by water?
103278.e: In a sawmill the water wheel drove a big saw. It was used to cut tree trunks into boards.
103278.m: Boards were sawn in the sawmill.

103279.q: What do you call the channel that carries the water to the mill wheel?
103279.e: The mill race was often specially branched off from a river. It carried the water to the wheel of the mill.
103279.m: A mill race brings water to the mill wheel.

103280.q: What does a hydroelectric power station use today instead of a mill wheel?
103280.e: A turbine is a modern kind of water wheel. It turns a generator, which makes electricity.
103280.m: Hydroelectric power stations make electricity with turbines.

103281.q: What material were old water wheels usually built from?
103281.e: In the past water wheels were mostly built of wood, because it could be found everywhere. Later there were also wheels made of iron.
103281.m: Old water wheels were mostly made of wood.

103282.q: What is a workshop called where a water wheel made a heavy hammer strike iron?
103282.e: In a hammer forge the water wheel lifted a big hammer and let it fall onto the red-hot iron. That is how tools were forged, for example.
103282.m: In a hammer forge, water power drove a hammer.

103283.q: What does the water wheel in the mill turn with the help of gear wheels?
103283.e: Gear wheels pass the turning of the water wheel into the inside of the mill. There they turn the millstone.
103283.m: Gear wheels pass on the power of the water wheel.

103284.q: How does a vacuum cleaner get the dust off the floor?
103284.e: A motor turns a fan, which sucks air in through the tube. The air carries the dust with it.
103284.m: A vacuum cleaner sucks up dust with the air.

103285.q: What holds back fine dust in the vacuum cleaner so that it doesn't get back into the air?
103285.e: A filter has very fine holes. The air gets through, but the fine dust doesn't.
103285.m: A filter holds back fine dust.

103286.q: Why does a vacuum cleaner suck less well when the bag is completely full?
a: The air can hardly flow through any more
103286.e: In a full bag there is hardly any room left for the air. When less air flows, less dust is carried along too.
103286.m: You change a full vacuum cleaner bag.

103287.q: What drives the fan in a vacuum cleaner?
103287.e: An electric motor turns the fan very fast. For that the vacuum cleaner needs electricity from the socket or a rechargeable battery.
103287.m: An electric motor drives the vacuum cleaner.

103288.q: What can you use to vacuum in narrow corners?
103288.e: The crevice tool is narrow and long. You use it to vacuum in corners, cracks and between cushions.
103288.m: In narrow corners you vacuum with the crevice tool.

103289.q: What did people use to clean carpets before the vacuum cleaner?
103289.e: In the past carpets were hung up outside and the dust was beaten out with a carpet beater. That was much harder work.
103289.m: In the past carpets were beaten.

103290.q: What turns round in a washing machine?
103290.e: The clothes lie in the drum. It turns back and forth so that the water with detergent gets everywhere.
103290.m: In a washing machine the drum turns.

103291.q: What does the washing machine do at the end during the spin?
103291.e: During the spin the drum turns very fast. This pushes the water out of the clothes through the holes in the drum.
103291.m: During the spin the drum turns very fast.

103292.q: What is the room called in many Swiss blocks of flats where the washing machine is?
103292.e: In many Swiss blocks of flats all the families share a laundry room in the cellar. A rota decides who may do their washing when.
103292.m: In many Swiss buildings the washing machine is in the laundry room.

103293.q: Why should you wash light and dark clothes separately?
a: Otherwise the machine gets too light
103293.e: New dark or colourful clothes can let colour out into the water. White washing then turns grey or discoloured.
103293.m: Light and dark clothes are washed separately.

103294.q: What do the little pictures on the label of a piece of clothing show?
103294.e: The care symbols on the label show, for example, how hot it can be washed. A washtub with a number gives the highest temperature.
103294.m: Care symbols show how to wash a piece of clothing.

103295.q: What can happen if you wash a wool jumper too hot?
103295.e: Wool felts in hot water with lots of movement. Then the jumper shrinks and gets smaller.

103296.q: What do you check in your trouser pockets before washing?
a: Whether there is still something in them
103296.e: Tissues, coins or pens in the pockets can damage the washing and the machine. That is why you empty the pockets first.
103296.m: Before washing you empty all pockets.

103298.q: What happens if something gets in the way of the lift door while it is closing?
103298.e: Light beams or sensors notice when something is in the way. Then the door opens again so that nobody gets trapped.
103298.m: A sensor opens the lift door when something is in the way.

103299.q: What does a cordless vacuum cleaner need to run?
103299.e: A rechargeable battery stores electricity like a battery you can charge again. That lets the vacuum cleaner run without a cable.
103299.m: A cordless vacuum cleaner doesn't need a cable.

103300.q: What is the big gear wheel at the front by the pedals of a bike called?
103300.e: The pedal cranks are attached to the front gear wheel. It is called the chainring because the chain runs over it.
103300.m: The front gear wheel on a bike is called the chainring.

103301.q: About how wide is the leaf rosette of the round-leaved sundew?
103301.e: The sundew is a small, inconspicuous plant. Its leaves lie in a flat rosette that is only a few centimetres wide.
103301.m: The sundew is a small plant.

103302.q: What does a sundew use to hold an insect?
103302.e: On the little hairs of its leaves there are drops that stick like glue. An insect that lands gets stuck.
103302.m: The sundew catches with sticky drops.

103303.q: What colour are the flowers of the round-leaved sundew?
103303.e: In summer, small white flowers grow on a thin stalk. They stand high above the trapping leaves.

103304.q: Why is the sundew called that?
a: It only flowers in the morning
103304.e: The drops on the leaves sparkle in the sun like dewdrops. That is how the plant got its name.
103304.m: The sundew's drops shine like dew.

103305.q: What does a sundew leaf do when an insect sticks to it?
a: It slowly bends around the insect
103305.e: The little hairs and the leaf slowly bend around the insect. That way the plant can digest it better.
103305.m: The sundew leaf rolls around its prey.

103306.q: Why does the sundew catch insects?
a: It has no roots at all
103306.e: In boggy soil there are hardly any nutrients. The insects give the sundew extra nutrients.
103306.m: Insects are extra fertiliser for the sundew.

103307.q: Are you allowed to simply pick sundew in Switzerland?
103307.e: The sundew is protected in Switzerland, and the moors are protected too. You may only look at it.

103308.q: Which group of plants does the sundew belong to?
103308.e: Plants that catch and digest animals are called carnivorous plants. The sundew is one of them.
103308.m: The sundew is a carnivorous plant.

103309.q: What colour are the hairs on the leaves of the round-leaved sundew usually?
103309.e: The hairs of the round-leaved sundew are usually red. This stands out a lot in the green moss.
103309.m: The sundew's hairs are usually red.

103310.q: What happens when you touch the leaves of the sensitive plant (mimosa)?
103310.e: The mimosa quickly folds up its small leaflets when touched. Sometimes even the whole leaf stalk droops.
103310.m: The mimosa folds up its leaves when touched.

103311.q: About how long does it take for the mimosa's leaves to open again after being touched?
103311.e: After a few minutes the leaflets slowly spread out again. Then the plant looks as it did before.
103311.m: The mimosa opens its leaves again after a few minutes.

103312.q: What do the mimosa's leaves do at night?
103312.e: The mimosa also folds up its leaves in the evening. In the morning it opens them again.
103312.m: The mimosa sleeps at night with folded leaves.

103313.q: Why does the mimosa probably fold up its leaves?
103313.e: An animal that wants to eat might get a fright when the leaves suddenly fold up. Also, the plant then looks smaller and less tasty.
103313.m: The mimosa protects itself with its folding leaves.

103314.q: What colour are the flowers of the mimosa whose leaves close when touched?
103314.e: The true mimosa has pink to lilac flowers. The yellow bunches sold in shops as “mimosa” are actually acacias.
103314.m: The true mimosa has pink flowers.

103315.q: What do the mimosa's flowers look like?
103315.e: Lots of tiny flowers sit close together and form a round, fluffy head. It looks like a small pompom.
103315.m: The mimosa has round flower heads.

103316.q: In German, what does it mean if you call a person a “Mimose” (a mimosa)?
103316.e: Because the plant reacts to even a light touch, sensitive people are sometimes called that in German. It is a figure of speech.
103316.m: In German, a “Mimose” is someone who is very sensitive.

103317.q: Where does the mimosa originally grow?
103317.e: The mimosa comes from the warm regions of the Americas. Today it grows in many tropical countries.
103317.m: The mimosa comes from the warm Americas.

103318.q: Where does the giant water lily Victoria grow in the wild?
103318.e: The giant water lily grows in calm waters in tropical South America. Its scientific name is Victoria amazonica.
103318.m: The giant water lily comes from the Amazon region.

103319.q: How big can the leaves of the giant water lily Victoria get?
103319.e: The round leaves float on the water and can be about 3 metres across. That is wider than a bed is long.
103319.m: The leaves of the giant water lily are huge.

103320.q: Who was the giant water lily Victoria named after?
103320.e: The plant was named after the English Queen Victoria in 1837. She had just become queen.
103320.m: The giant water lily bears the name of a queen.

103321.q: Who can a large leaf of the giant water lily carry if the weight is spread out well?
103321.e: The leaves are built very sturdily. In the past, small children were put on a board on top of them for fun.
103321.m: A giant water lily leaf can carry a surprising amount.

103322.q: When do the flowers of the giant water lily open?
103322.e: The flower opens at sunset and then gives off a scent. That is how it attracts beetles.
103322.m: The giant water lily opens its flower in the evening.

103323.q: What shape are the leaves of the giant water lily?
a: Long like a blade of grass
103323.e: The leaves of the giant water lily are round and float flat on the water. They look like giant plates.
103323.m: The giant water lily has round leaves like plates.

103324.q: What does the edge of a giant water lily leaf look like?
a: It is completely flat and thin
103324.e: The edge of the leaf is turned up like a baking tray. That way hardly any water splashes onto the leaf.
103324.m: The giant water lily has a turned-up leaf edge.

103325.q: What does the giant water lily have on the underside of its leaves?
103325.e: The underside and the stalks are covered in spines. They protect the plant from fish and other animals that want to eat it.
103325.m: The giant water lily protects its leaves with spines.

103326.q: Why don't the huge leaves of the giant water lily sink?
a: They have lots of air pockets
103326.e: Between the thick leaf veins there are spaces full of air. That is why the leaves are light and float.
103326.m: Air in the leaf makes the giant water lily float.

103327.q: What does the titan arum smell of when it flowers?
103327.e: The titan arum gives off a very strong, disgusting smell. That is why it is also called the “corpse flower”.
103327.m: The flowering titan arum stinks terribly.

103328.q: How tall can the flower spike of the titan arum grow?
103328.e: The flower spike can grow over 3 metres tall. It is the largest unbranched flower spike in the world.
103328.m: The titan arum has a huge flower spike.

103329.q: Which island is the titan arum's home?
103329.e: The titan arum grows wild only in the rainforest on Sumatra in Indonesia. In Switzerland you can sometimes see it in botanical gardens.
103329.m: The titan arum comes from Sumatra.

103330.q: About how long does a titan arum flower spike bloom?
103330.e: The flowering only lasts about 24 to 36 hours. That is why lots of people hurry to the botanical garden when it blooms.
103330.m: The titan arum flowers only very briefly.

103331.q: Why does the flowering titan arum smell so strongly?
103331.e: The smell attracts beetles and flies that normally look for carrion. These insects pollinate the flowers.
103331.m: The titan arum's stench calls its pollinators.

103332.q: How often does a titan arum flower?
103332.e: The plant needs a lot of energy for the huge flower. That is why it only flowers every few years.
103332.m: The titan arum flowers very rarely.

103333.q: What does the titan arum have underground?
103333.e: Underground there is a large tuber that can weigh over 90 kilograms. The plant stores nutrients in it.
103333.m: The titan arum stores its energy in a tuber.

103334.q: What happens to the titan arum's flower spike while it is flowering?
103334.e: The spike in the middle heats up to about the same temperature as a human. The warmth helps to spread the smell.
103334.m: The flowering titan arum heats up.

103335.q: What does the titan arum grow in the years when it doesn't flower?
103335.e: In the years without flowers only one leaf grows. It looks like a small tree and can be several metres tall.
103335.m: The titan arum forms a single giant leaf.
