104896.e: More substances are dissolved in the cell sap of the root hairs than in the water in the soil. So water flows into the cells by osmosis.
104896.m: Water gets into the root hairs by osmosis.

104897.q: What do root hairs on a cress seedling look like to the naked eye?
104897.e: On sprouting cress you can see a white, fluffy coating on the root. These are the root hairs, not mould.
104897.m: The white fluff on cress roots is made of root hairs.

a: A protective cap on the root tip
A leaf on the root collar
The bark of a tree trunk
104898.e: The root cap sits like a hat on the tip of every growing root. It protects the delicate tip as it pushes into the soil.
104898.m: The root cap sits like a hat on the root tip.

104899.q: What does the root cap mainly protect?
a: The dividing tissue of the root tip
The root hairs on old roots
104899.e: Behind the cap lies the growth tissue, where new cells keep dividing. Without protection it would be damaged by grains of soil.
104899.m: The root cap protects the delicate growth tissue of the tip.

104900.q: What can you best compare the root cap with?
104900.e: The root cap sits like a hat on the root tip. It protects the tip while the root pushes through the soil.
104900.m: The root cap is like a hat for the root tip.

104901.q: What do the cells of the root cap release so that the root slides through the soil more easily?
104901.e: The outer cells of the root cap make a slime. It works like a lubricant between the root and the soil particles.
104901.m: Slime from the root cap lets the root slide through the soil.

104902.q: What happens to the outer cells of the root cap?
a: They are rubbed off and replaced from inside
They turn into a woody trunk
104902.e: As the root pushes into the soil, the outer cells are constantly scraped off. New cells keep forming from the inside.
104902.m: The root cap constantly renews itself from the inside.

104903.q: Which roots have a root cap?
104903.e: Not just the main root but every growing side root has a root cap at its tip. So a root system has a great many of them.
104903.m: Side roots also have a root cap at their tip.

104904.q: How does a root know which direction to grow in?
104904.e: Heavy little grains sink to the bottom in the root cap. This way the root can tell where down is.

104905.q: A seed is planted upside down in the soil. Which way does its root grow?
104905.e: Roots always grow in the direction of gravity. Even if the seed is lying the wrong way, the root bends downwards.

104906.q: What is a vascular bundle in plants?
104906.e: Vascular bundles are long strands that connect the root, shoot and leaves. Water, minerals and sugar are transported in them.
104906.m: Vascular bundles are the transport strands of the plant.

104907.q: What do the vascular bundles carry from the roots up into the leaves?
104907.e: Water with dissolved minerals rises in one part of the vascular bundles. In another part, sugar from the leaves is distributed.
104907.m: Vascular bundles carry water and minerals upwards.

104908.q: Which land plants have no true vascular bundles?
104908.e: Mosses have no true transport tissues. That is why they stay small and need damp places.
104908.m: Mosses have no true vascular bundles and so stay small.

104909.q: How are the vascular bundles arranged in the stem of a dicot?
104909.e: In dicots such as the sunflower the vascular bundles lie in a ring in the stem. You can see this well in a cross-section.
104909.m: In dicots the vascular bundles lie in a ring.

104910.q: How are the vascular bundles arranged in the stem of maize and other monocots?
a: Only on the outside in the bark
104910.e: In monocots such as maize the vascular bundles are scattered across the whole cross-section. You can see this well if you cut a maize stem across.
104910.m: In monocots the vascular bundles are scattered.

104911.q: What are the visible veins in a leaf?
104911.e: The leaf veins contain vascular bundles. They bring water into the leaf and carry sugar away.
104911.m: Leaf veins are vascular bundles in the leaf.

104912.q: What does the cambium in a tree trunk make possible?
a: The trunk getting thicker every year
104912.e: The cambium is a thin layer of dividing cells. It forms new wood every year, and this creates the growth rings.
104912.m: The cambium makes the tree trunk grow thicker.

104913.q: What becomes visible if you stand celery in water with food colouring?
104913.e: The coloured water rises upwards in the vascular bundles. In a cross-section you can then see coloured dots.
104913.m: With dye you can make the path of water in the vascular bundles visible.

104914.q: What does the xylem carry in a plant?
104914.e: The xylem carries water with dissolved minerals from the root up into the leaves. The transport goes upwards.
104914.m: The xylem carries water up from the root.

104916.q: What state are the water-carrying cells of the xylem in when they are working?
104916.e: The conducting cells die and their contents disappear. What is left are hollow tubes that the water flows through.
104916.m: The water pipes in the xylem are hollow, dead cells.

104917.q: Which substance strengthens the cell walls in the xylem and makes wood hard?
104917.e: Lignin is laid down in the cell walls and makes them firm and able to withstand pressure. This process is called lignification.
104917.m: Lignin makes cell walls hard and woody.

104918.q: What pulls the water in the xylem right up into the treetop?
104918.e: Water evaporates from the leaves through the stomata. This creates a pull that draws more water up the xylem.
104918.m: Evaporation from the leaves pulls water upwards.

104919.q: How can you show that a plant carries water upwards?
a: Stand a white flower in coloured water
Put the flower in the fridge
Put the flower in a dark cupboard
104919.e: The colour rises with the water through the tubes in the stem. After a while the petals change colour.
104919.m: Coloured water shows how water is transported in the plant.

104920.q: Why is the earlywood formed in spring paler than the latewood?
104920.e: In spring the tree needs a lot of water and forms wide, thin-walled cells. In late summer narrow, thick-walled cells form, which look darker.
104920.m: Earlywood is pale because its cells are wide and thin-walled.

104921.q: What is the inner, often darker part of a trunk called, which no longer carries water?
104921.e: In many trees, such as oak or larch, only the outer part of the wood, the sapwood, still carries water. The inner part becomes heartwood, which is often darker and especially durable.
104921.m: The heartwood inside a trunk no longer carries water.

104923.q: What does the phloem mainly carry?
104923.e: Sugar is made in the leaves by photosynthesis. The phloem distributes this dissolved sugar throughout the whole plant.
104923.m: The phloem distributes the sugar from the leaves.

104925.q: What are the conducting cells in the phloem called?
104925.e: Sieve tubes are cells lined up end to end with sieve-like cross walls. The sugary sap flows through the pores.
104925.m: In the phloem the sugary sap flows through sieve tubes.

104926.q: Where is the phloem in a tree?
a: Right in the centre of the trunk
104926.e: In trees the phloem lies as a thin layer directly under the bark. That is why damaged bark is dangerous for the tree.
104926.m: In a tree the phloem lies directly under the bark.

104927.q: In which direction does the sap flow in the phloem?
a: Up or down, depending on need
Not at all, it stays still
104927.e: The sugary sap flows from where sugar is made or stored to where it is needed. That can be a root below or a fruit above.
104927.m: In the phloem the sap flows to where sugar is needed.

104928.q: Unlike the phloem, which transport tissue carries water up from the roots?
104928.e: The xylem, also called wood tissue, carries water and minerals upwards. The phloem, on the other hand, distributes the sugar from the leaves.
104928.m: Xylem carries water, phloem carries sugar.

104929.q: Which small insects pierce the phloem and suck the sugary sap?
104929.e: Aphids pierce the sieve tubes precisely with their mouthparts. They release the extra sugar again as honeydew.
104929.m: Aphids tap into the phloem with their mouthparts.

104930.q: Why does a tree die if you remove the bark all the way round down to the wood?
a: The roots no longer get any sugar
The wood can no longer carry water
The leaves fall off at once
104930.e: When a tree is ring-barked, the sugar-carrying layer directly under the bark is removed too. The roots no longer receive sugar and slowly starve.
104930.m: Without a ring of bark, a tree’s roots starve.

104931.q: What is the sticky, sweet liquid called that aphids release after sucking phloem sap?
104931.e: The sap in the phloem contains a lot of sugar. Aphids release the extra sugar as honeydew, which ants love to eat.

104932.q: What kind of tissue is the cambium?
a: A growth tissue that can divide
A protective tissue made of cork
104932.e: The cells of the cambium can divide again and again. Tissues like this are called growth tissues or meristems.
104932.m: The cambium is a growth tissue with dividing cells.

104933.q: Where is the cambium in a tree trunk?
a: As a thin layer between wood and bark
Right in the middle of the trunk
On the surface of the outer bark
104933.e: The cambium surrounds the wood like a thin coat and lies directly under the bark. It is often only a few layers of cells thick.
104933.m: The cambium lies like a thin coat between wood and bark.

104934.q: What does the cambium form on its inner side?
104934.e: The cambium releases most of its new cells towards the inside. These become new wood.
104934.m: On the inside the cambium forms wood.

104935.q: What does the cambium form on its outer side?
104935.e: Towards the outside the cambium releases cells that become bast. The sugar-carrying tissue lies in the bast.
104935.m: On the outside the cambium forms bast.

104936.q: Why do growth rings form in a tree trunk?
a: The cambium forms different wood depending on the season
The tree turns round once every year
A new bark grows inwards every year
The rain colours the wood every year
104936.e: In spring and summer the cambium is active and forms wood; in winter it rests. This creates a visible ring every year.
104936.m: Each growth ring stands for one year of the cambium’s work.

104937.q: What is the method called that works out the age of wood from its growth rings?
104937.e: Dendrochronology compares patterns of growth rings and can often date wood to the exact year. The Greek word dendron means tree.
104937.m: Dendrochronology reads age from growth rings.

104938.q: Why do palm trees have no true growth rings?
a: They lack a cambium for growing thicker
They are cut down every year
Their trunk is made of leaves
104938.e: Palms are monocots and have no ring-shaped cambium. That is why they do not grow thicker with growth rings.
104938.m: Without a cambium a plant forms no growth rings.

104939.q: When grafting fruit trees, what must you make sure of so that the scion and rootstock grow together?
a: Both must have the same number of leaves
The bark must be removed first
104939.e: Only the cambium can form new cells and join the wound. That is why the cambium layers of both parts must be in contact.
104939.m: When grafting, the cambium layers must touch.

104940.q: Which part of the plant is the shoot axis?
104940.e: The shoot axis is the part of the plant that carries leaves and flowers. In herbs it is called the stem, in trees the trunk.
104940.m: The shoot axis is the stem or trunk of a plant.

104941.q: What job does the shoot axis do?
104941.e: The shoot axis holds the leaves up to the light. At the same time it connects the root and the leaves and carries substances between them.
104941.m: The shoot axis carries the leaves and transports substances.

104942.q: What are the points on the shoot axis where leaves are attached called?
104942.e: The leaves grow from the nodes. Buds are often found there too.
104942.m: Leaves grow at the nodes of the shoot axis.

104943.q: What happens to a plant when the sections between the leaf joints on its stem become especially long?
104943.e: The sections between two nodes are called internodes. If they are long, the plant grows tall, for example when it is reaching for light in the shade.
104943.m: Long sections between the nodes make a plant tall and stretched.

104944.q: What is the usually hollow shoot axis of grasses, divided by nodes, called?
104944.e: Grasses and cereals have a culm. It is usually hollow and strengthened by thickened nodes.
104944.m: The shoot axis of grasses is called a culm.

104945.q: From a botanical point of view, what is a potato tuber?
104945.e: Potato tubers grow on underground shoots. Their eyes are buds, which shows that they are parts of a shoot.
104945.m: The potato is a stem tuber, not a root.

104946.q: Which part of the plant carries out photosynthesis in most cacti?
104946.e: In cacti the leaves have turned into spines. The thick, green stem stores water and carries out photosynthesis.
104946.m: In cacti the green stem does the photosynthesis.

104947.q: What are the long side shoots above ground called, with which strawberries form new plants?
104947.e: Strawberries form thin shoots that creep over the ground. New young plants take root at their ends.

104948.q: Botanically, what is a piece of ginger root?
104948.e: Ginger forms an underground shoot that grows sideways, called a rhizome. You can see nodes and buds on it.
104948.m: Ginger is a rhizome, an underground shoot.

a: Roots that grow out of the shoot above ground
Roots that only grow in water
104949.e: Aerial roots grow above the ground from the trunk, branches or stem. They can have very different jobs.
104949.m: Aerial roots grow out of the shoot above the ground.

104950.q: What does ivy use its short aerial roots for?
a: To cling to walls and trees
To suck water out of the wall
104950.e: The clinging roots of ivy grip the tiniest bumps. Ivy takes in water through its roots in the soil.

104951.q: Which popular houseplant grows on trees in the wild and has silvery-green aerial roots?
104951.e: Many orchids, such as Phalaenopsis, grow on branches in the rainforest. Their aerial roots take in rainwater and moisture.
104951.m: Orchids hold on to trees with aerial roots.

104952.q: What are the breathing roots that stick straight up out of the mud in mangroves for?
104952.e: The mud in mangrove forests contains hardly any oxygen. The breathing roots that stick out fetch air for the roots in the ground.
104952.m: Mangroves breathe through roots that stick out of the mud.

104953.q: Which crop forms prop roots on its lower stem that grow at a slant into the ground?
104953.e: Maize forms aerial roots at its lower nodes that grow into the ground. They support the tall plant against the wind.
104953.m: Maize props itself up with aerial roots at the base of its stem.

104954.q: Which tropical plant wraps its aerial roots around a host tree until the tree dies?
104954.e: The strangler fig sprouts high up on a tree and sends aerial roots downwards. These wrap around the trunk and take away its light and space.
104954.m: The strangler fig wraps its host tree in aerial roots.

104955.q: In which tree do aerial roots grow from the branches into the ground and become new trunks?
104955.e: The banyan tree, a kind of fig from India, forms aerial roots on its branches. When they reach the ground, they thicken into supporting trunks.
104955.m: In the banyan tree, aerial roots become new trunks.

104956.q: What are plants called that grow on other plants without touching the soil and often have aerial roots?
104956.e: Epiphytes use other plants only as a base to sit on. Unlike parasites, they do not take nutrients from them.
104956.m: Epiphytes grow on other plants without harming them.

104957.q: Which vegetable is a storage root?
104957.e: The carrot is the thickened main root of the plant. It stores sugar and other nutrients in it.
104957.m: The carrot is a thickened storage root.

104958.q: What supplies do plants mainly store in storage roots?
104958.e: Storage roots hold nutrients that the plant has made in its leaves. Usually these are starch or sugar.
104958.m: Storage roots are larders for starch and sugar.

104959.q: Why does a biennial plant such as the carrot form a storage root in its first year?
a: To flower and make seeds in its second year
104959.e: In its first year the plant collects supplies in its root. In its second year it uses this energy to form flowers and seeds.
104959.m: Biennial plants collect supplies for flowering in their first year.

104960.q: Which of these vegetables is a true root tuber?
104960.e: The sweet potato stores its starch in thickened roots. Jerusalem artichoke and kohlrabi, on the other hand, are thickened shoots, and the onion is made of thickened leaves.
104960.m: The sweet potato is a root tuber.

104961.q: Which starchy storage root is a staple food in many tropical countries?
104961.e: Cassava forms large, starchy root tubers. Raw it is poisonous, but cooked it is an important food for millions of people.
104961.m: Cassava is an important storage root of the tropics.

104962.q: Why do people dig up dahlia tubers in autumn?
104962.e: Dahlias come from Mexico and cannot survive frost. That is why their tubers spend the winter in a cool, frost-free place.
104962.m: Dahlia tubers must spend the winter free from frost.

104963.q: Which white winter vegetable is a storage root like the carrot?
104963.e: The parsnip forms a thick, white storage root. Leek, Brussels sprouts and fennel, on the other hand, are leaves or buds.
104963.m: The parsnip is a white storage root.

104964.q: What do you call a storage root that develops from the thickened main root?
104964.e: If the main root is strongly thickened, it is called a beet. Examples are the carrot and the sugar beet.
104964.m: A thickened main root is called a beet.

104965.q: Which substance can you use to detect starch in a storage root?
104965.e: Iodine solution turns starch blue-black. This lets you test whether a root stores starch as a supply.

a: The upthrust equals the weight of the displaced liquid
Every object falls at the same speed
Heat always flows from cold to warm
Light is always reflected by water
104966.e: An object in a liquid pushes liquid aside. It feels an upward force that is exactly as large as the weight of this displaced liquid.
104966.m: Upthrust equals the weight of the displaced liquid.

104967.q: Which word is Archimedes said to have shouted after his discovery in the bath?
104967.e: Eureka is Greek and means “I have found it”. Archimedes is said to have noticed while bathing that his body pushed water aside.

104968.q: Why does a heavy steel ship float?
a: It displaces as much water as it weighs
The salt in the sea carries it
104968.e: Thanks to its hollow shape, the hull pushes aside a large amount of water. If this water weighs as much as the ship, the upthrust is big enough.
104968.m: A ship floats because it displaces enough water.

104969.q: When a stone is dipped in, it displaces 3 litres of water. What is the mass of the displaced water?
104969.e: One litre of water has a mass of about 1 kg. So 3 litres times 1 kg per litre gives 3 kg.
104969.m: One litre of water has a mass of about one kilogram.

104970.q: When does an object float on water?
a: When its density is lower than that of water
When it weighs more than 1 kg
When it is made of metal
104970.e: If an object's density is lower than water's, the upthrust becomes larger than its weight before it is fully under water. That is why it floats.
104970.m: Anything less dense than water floats.

104971.q: Why is it easier to float in the very salty Dead Sea than in a Swiss lake?
a: Salt water has a greater density
104971.e: Salt water is denser than fresh water. The displaced water therefore weighs more and the upthrust is greater.
104971.m: Dense salt water gives more upthrust.

104972.q: According to Archimedes' principle, why does a hot-air balloon rise?
a: The cold air it displaces is heavier than the balloon
The fire pushes it like a rocket
The wind pushes it from below
104972.e: The principle also applies to gases. The balloon with hot, light air displaces cooler, heavier surrounding air and so gets upthrust.
104972.m: There is upthrust in air too.

104973.q: An object with a mass of 5 kg displaces 2 litres under water. How heavy does it seem under water?
104973.e: The upthrust equals the weight of 2 litres of water, which is about 2 kg. So it only seems to weigh 5 kg minus 2 kg, which is 3 kg.
104973.m: Under water an object seems lighter by the amount of upthrust.

104974.e: Translated, Eureka means “I have found it”. Today people shout it when they suddenly have a solution.

104975.q: Which language does the word “Eureka” come from?
104975.e: Archimedes spoke Greek, like many scholars of his time. Eureka is a form of the Ancient Greek verb for “to find”.
104975.m: Eureka is an Ancient Greek word.

104976.q: According to legend, where did Archimedes shout “Eureka”?
104976.e: When he climbed into the full tub and water overflowed, the solution is said to have come to him. According to legend he then shouted “Eureka”.
104976.m: Archimedes is said to have had his idea in the bath.

104977.q: According to the legend, where is Archimedes supposed to have shouted “Eureka”?
104977.e: When Archimedes climbed into the tub, the water rose. This gave him the idea of how to measure the volume of an object.

104978.q: What was Archimedes supposed to find out in the Eureka story?
a: Whether a crown was made of pure gold
How far away the Moon is
104978.e: The king suspected that the goldsmith had mixed in silver. Archimedes was to check this without damaging the crown.
104978.m: Archimedes was to check whether a golden crown was genuine.

104979.q: How could Archimedes test the crown without destroying it?
a: He compared the water it displaced with that of pure gold
He weighed it on the Moon
104979.e: Silver of the same weight has a larger volume than gold and displaces more water. If the crown displaces more water than a lump of gold of the same weight, it is not pure.
104979.m: Water displacement can be used to measure an object's volume.

104980.e: Archimedes lived in the 3rd century BC in Syracuse on Sicily. He was one of the greatest mathematicians and inventors of the ancient world.

104981.q: Which US state has “Eureka” as its motto?
104981.e: California has “Eureka” as its state motto. It recalls the gold finds at the time of the gold rush in the 19th century.

104982.q: Which profession is linked with the Hippocratic Oath?
104982.e: The Hippocratic Oath is a pledge for doctors. It describes how they should behave towards sick people.
104982.m: The Hippocratic Oath is a promise made by doctors.

104983.q: Which ancient doctor is the Hippocratic Oath named after?
104983.e: The oath bears the name of the Greek doctor Hippocrates. Whether he wrote it himself is, however, uncertain.
104983.m: The Hippocratic Oath is named after Hippocrates.

104984.q: Which title of honour is Hippocrates often given?
104984.e: Hippocrates is regarded as the founder of medicine as a science. That is why he is often called the Father of Medicine.
104984.m: Hippocrates is regarded as the Father of Medicine.

104985.q: Which country did Hippocrates come from?
104985.e: Hippocrates came from the Greek island of Kos. There was a famous school of medicine there.

104986.q: Which duty of doctors is already in the Hippocratic Oath?
104986.e: In the oath, the doctor promises to keep silent about what he learns during treatment. This duty of confidentiality still applies today.
104986.m: Doctors must keep what they hear confidential.

104987.q: What does a doctor mainly promise in the Hippocratic Oath?
a: To help the sick and not harm them
To earn as much money as possible
104987.e: The wellbeing of the sick is at the heart of the oath. Doctors should help and not deliberately harm anyone.
104987.m: Doctors promise to help the sick and not harm them.

104988.q: Which symbol, a staff with a snake, still stands for medicine today?
104988.e: The rod is named after Asclepius, the Greek god of healing, who is also named in the Hippocratic Oath. You often see it on pharmacies and ambulances.
104988.m: The Rod of Asclepius is the symbol of medicine.

104989.q: What was new about the medicine of Hippocrates?
a: He looked for natural causes of illness
He healed only with magic spells
104989.e: Hippocrates did not see illnesses as a punishment from the gods. He observed sick people closely and looked for natural causes.
104989.m: Hippocrates explained illnesses with natural causes.

104990.e: Hippocrates was born around 460 BC and died around 370 BC. So he lived in classical Greece.
104990.m: Hippocrates lived in the 5th and 4th centuries BC.

104991.q: Roughly how long did the geocentric model worked out in the 2nd century AD remain the accepted teaching?
104991.e: The model was created in the 2nd century AD, and a new picture only became accepted in the 16th and 17th centuries. That is about 1400 years in between.
104991.m: The ancient geocentric model lasted about 1400 years.

104992.q: Which scholar from Alexandria summed up the geocentric view of the universe in the 2nd century AD?
104992.e: Claudius Ptolemy described the movements of the heavenly bodies around the Earth in great detail. His model shaped astronomy in Europe and the Arab world.
104992.m: Ptolemy described the geocentric view of the universe in detail.

104993.q: What was at the centre of Ptolemy's geocentric view of the universe?
104993.e: Ptolemy described a view of the universe in which the Sun, Moon and planets circle the Earth. His work was preserved by Arab scholars.
104993.m: In the geocentric view, the Earth is at the centre.

104994.q: Which astronomer put the Sun at the centre in a book in 1543?
104994.e: In 1543 Copernicus published his work on the revolutions of the heavenly bodies. In it, the planets circle the Sun.
104994.m: Copernicus put the Sun at the centre.

104995.q: Which scientist discovered moons orbiting Jupiter with a telescope in 1610, which spoke against the geocentric view?
104995.e: Galileo saw that moons circle Jupiter and not the Earth. This made it clear that not everything goes round the Earth.
104995.m: Galileo found Jupiter's moons with a telescope.

104996.q: What did people observe about planets in the sky that was hard to explain with the geocentric view?
a: They sometimes seem to move backwards
They only shine during the day
They always stay in the same place
104996.e: Planets such as Mars sometimes seem to make a loop in the sky. Ptolemy needed complicated extra circles to explain this.
104996.m: The loops of the planets were hard to explain.

104997.q: Which famous philosopher saw the Earth at the centre, surrounded by heavenly spheres?
104997.e: Aristotle imagined the heavenly bodies on transparent spheres around the Earth. His teaching shaped thinking for many centuries.
104997.m: Aristotle saw the Earth at the centre of the world.

104998.q: Why did people think the geocentric view was right for so long?
a: The Sun and stars seem to move round the Earth
The Earth is the largest heavenly body
You could never see the Sun
The planets are invisible at night
104998.e: From the Earth it looks as if the Sun, Moon and stars circle around us. You cannot feel the Earth turning.
104998.m: What we see seems to suggest the Earth stands still.

104999.q: What is the view of the universe that replaced the geocentric view called?
104999.e: Helios is the Greek word for sun. In the heliocentric view, the Earth and the other planets circle the Sun.
104999.m: The heliocentric view puts the Sun at the centre.

105000.e: Galen was one of the most famous doctors of the ancient world. He wrote a great many books about medicine.
105000.m: Galen was a famous doctor of the ancient world.

105001.q: When did the doctor Galen live?
a: In ancient times, in the age of the Romans
In the Middle Ages, in the age of knights
105001.e: Galen lived in the 2nd century AD. He came from Asia Minor and later worked mainly in Rome.
105001.m: Galen was a doctor in the Roman Empire.

105002.q: Whom did Galen treat at the start of his career in Pergamon?
105002.e: In Pergamon, Galen was the doctor for the gladiators. From their wounds he learnt a lot about how the body is built.
105002.m: Galen gained experience as a doctor to gladiators.

105003.q: In which city did Galen later work as a respected doctor?
105003.e: Galen moved to Rome and even treated emperors there. He was one of the most famous doctors of his time.
105003.m: Galen was a famous doctor in Rome.

105004.q: Which medical theory did Galen develop a great deal?
a: The theory of the four humours
105004.e: According to the theory of the four humours, you stay healthy if blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile are in balance. Galen made this theory very influential.
105004.m: Galen spread the theory of the four bodily humours.

105005.q: Why did Galen mainly study animals such as monkeys and pigs?
a: Opening human corpses was not allowed in Rome
105005.e: In the Roman Empire, dissecting humans was forbidden. Galen applied what he learnt from animals to humans, which led to some mistakes.
105005.m: Galen learnt anatomy mainly from animals.

105006.q: Why were mistakes later found in Galen's descriptions?
a: Doctors now examined human bodies themselves
105006.e: In the 16th century, doctors such as Vesalius examined human bodies themselves. They saw that some things were different from what Galen had worked out from animals.
105006.m: Careful examination uncovered mistakes in old teachings.

105007.q: Which branch of pharmacy is named after Galen?
105007.e: Galenics is the study of making medicines in forms such as tablets and ointments. Its name recalls Galen.

a: She was a mathematician and philosopher
She was a queen of Egypt
105008.e: Hypatia taught mathematics, astronomy and philosophy. She is one of the first female mathematicians known by name.
105008.m: Hypatia was an important mathematician of the ancient world.

105009.q: In which city did Hypatia teach?
105009.e: Hypatia lived and taught in Alexandria in Egypt, an important centre of science in the ancient world.

105010.e: Hypatia was born around AD 355 and died in AD 415 or 416. So she lived in late antiquity.

105011.q: Which subject did Hypatia teach besides mathematics and philosophy?
105011.e: Hypatia also taught astronomy and explained how stars and planets move.

105012.q: Which astronomical instrument is Hypatia said to have explained to her pupil Synesius?
105012.e: In a letter, Synesius mentions an astrolabe that he built with Hypatia's help. It could be used to find the position of stars.
105012.m: An astrolabe was used to find the position of stars.

105013.q: What on the Moon is named after Hypatia?
105013.e: A lunar crater bears the name Hypatia. This is how important scientists are honoured.

105014.q: Why do we know little today about Hypatia's own writings?
a: Almost all her works are lost
She wrote in a secret code
Her books have not been translated yet
105014.e: Hardly anything of Hypatia's works has survived directly. We know her mainly from reports by other authors.
105014.m: We know Hypatia's works almost only from other people's reports.

105015.q: In which century did Hero of Alexandria live?
105015.e: Hero probably lived in Alexandria in the 1st century AD. He was a mathematician and engineer.
105015.m: Hero was an engineer of the 1st century AD.

105016.q: What can you calculate with Hero's formula?
a: The area of a triangle from its three sides
105016.e: Hero's formula gives the area of a triangle when only the three side lengths are known. You don't need a height.
105016.m: Hero's formula gives the area of a triangle from its sides.

105017.q: A triangle has sides of 3 cm, 4 cm and 5 cm. What area does Hero's formula give?
105017.e: Half the perimeter is s = 6. The area is the square root of 6 · 3 · 2 · 1 = 36, so 6 cm².
105017.m: A triangle with sides of 3, 4 and 5 cm has an area of 6 cm².

105018.q: Which calculation does Hero's method approach step by step?
a: The square root of a number
The sum of all prime numbers
105018.e: In Hero's method you keep taking the mean of an estimate and the number divided by the estimate. That way you get closer and closer to the root.
105018.m: Hero's method is used to calculate square roots.

105019.q: What did the early coin-operated machine described by Hero give out when a coin was put in?
105019.e: When a coin fell onto a small pan, a valve opened briefly and some holy water flowed out. The device is regarded as one of the first vending machines.
105019.m: Hero's coin machine gave out holy water.

105020.q: What did Hero make happen as if by magic, using fire on an altar?
105020.e: The fire heated air, which pushed water into a vessel. Its weight pulled the temple doors open by means of ropes.
105020.m: Hero used heated air to move doors.

a: By air pressure without a pump
With the muscle power of animals
105021.e: Falling water pushes air into a second container. This air presses water upwards out of a nozzle, without any pump.
105021.m: Hero's fountain squirts by air pressure alone.

105022.q: Hero built a ball that was turned by escaping steam. Which later invention also uses steam power?
105022.e: Almost 2000 years ago, Hero's steam ball already showed that steam can move things. But steam power was only put to use much later in steam engines.
105022.m: Hero showed early on that steam can drive something.

105023.e: The aeolipile is a hollow ball that can turn and out of which steam escapes. It is one of the oldest known heat engines.
105023.m: The aeolipile is an ancient steam ball.

105024.q: From which period does the aeolipile come?
105024.e: The aeolipile was described about 2000 years ago in ancient Alexandria. It is also called Hero's engine.
105024.m: The aeolipile is an invention from ancient times.

105025.q: The aeolipile is regarded as an early form of which machine?
105025.e: In the aeolipile, escaping steam drives a turning movement directly, without any pistons. That is why it is regarded as a simple, early steam turbine.
105025.m: The aeolipile is regarded as a forerunner of the steam turbine.

105026.q: Which physical principle makes the aeolipile turn?
105026.e: The steam shoots out in one direction and the ball is pushed in the opposite direction. Rockets fly according to the same principle.
105026.m: The aeolipile turns by recoil, like a rocket.

105027.q: Which Greek god is the aeolipile named after?
a: Aeolus, the god of the winds
Poseidon, the god of the sea
105027.e: The name combines the wind god Aeolus with the Latin word pila, meaning ball. So it means a wind ball.
105027.m: The aeolipile is a ball of the wind god Aeolus.

105028.q: As far as we know today, what was the aeolipile used for in ancient times?
105028.e: No practical use as a working machine is known. The aeolipile was more likely shown as an astonishing showpiece.
105028.m: In ancient times the aeolipile was more a showpiece than a machine.

105029.q: Which energy conversion does the aeolipile show?
105029.e: The fire supplies heat, which turns water into steam. The steam sets the ball moving.
105029.m: In the aeolipile, heat becomes movement.

105030.q: How are the outlet tubes of an aeolipile pointed?
a: Into the inside of the ball
105030.e: The tubes are fitted opposite each other and point in opposite directions. That way both jets of steam make the ball turn the same way.
105030.m: Tubes bent in opposite directions make the ball spin.

a: An ancient calculator for movements in the sky
105031.e: The mechanism used gearwheels to calculate the positions of the Sun and Moon. It is regarded as the oldest known analogue computer.
105031.m: The Antikythera mechanism is an ancient analogue computer.

105032.q: Where was the Antikythera mechanism found?
a: In a shipwreck off a Greek island
In a cave in the Alps
105032.e: It lay in an ancient wreck off the small island of Antikythera. It is named after this island.
105032.m: The mechanism comes from a wreck off Antikythera.

105033.q: Who discovered the wreck containing the mechanism around 1900?
105033.e: Sponge divers from Symi came across the wreck around 1900. The mechanism was recovered in 1901.
105033.m: Sponge divers found the Antikythera wreck.

105034.q: What are the gearwheels of the Antikythera mechanism made of?
105034.e: The gearwheels were made of bronze and sat in a wooden case. The seawater has badly corroded them.
105034.m: The mechanism is made of bronze gearwheels.

105035.q: Roughly how many of the mechanism's gearwheels have survived?
105035.e: About 30 gearwheels have survived. There were probably a few more originally.
105035.m: About 30 of the mechanism's gearwheels have survived.

105036.q: Which events in the sky could the Antikythera mechanism predict?
105036.e: A dial on the back showed eclipses long in advance. It was based on a cycle of just over 18 years.

105037.q: In which museum is the Antikythera mechanism displayed today?
105037.e: The fragments are shown in the National Archaeological Museum in Athens. You can also see reconstructions there.
105037.m: The mechanism is in Athens today.

105038.q: Which technique made it possible from 2005 to read inscriptions inside the mechanism?
105038.e: A research team scanned the fragments with X-ray computed tomography. This revealed hidden gearwheels and texts.
105038.m: X-ray images let researchers see inside the mechanism.

105039.q: What did Eratosthenes calculate astonishingly accurately?
105039.e: Eratosthenes needed only simple measurements and geometry for this. His result came astonishingly close to today's value of about 40,000 kilometres.
105039.m: Eratosthenes calculated the Earth's circumference astonishingly accurately.

105040.q: What did Eratosthenes compare in Alexandria and Syene to calculate the Earth's circumference?
a: The shadow of the midday sun
105040.e: At midday the Sun cast practically no shadow in Syene, but it did in Alexandria. From the difference in angle he worked out the curve of the Earth.
105040.m: Eratosthenes used shadows to measure the Earth.

105041.q: In which country were the cities of Alexandria and Syene, where Eratosthenes made his measurement?
105041.e: Alexandria lies on Egypt's Mediterranean coast, Syene further south on the Nile. Today Syene is called Aswan.
105041.m: Eratosthenes measured the Earth in Egypt.

105042.q: Eratosthenes' angle was 1/50 of a circle and the distance was 5000 stadia. What circumference of the Earth does this give?
105042.e: If 5000 stadia equal one fiftieth of the circle, the whole circle is 50 times as long. So 50 · 5000 = 250,000 stadia.

105043.q: Which famous institution did Eratosthenes run?
105043.e: Eratosthenes became head of the Library of Alexandria. It was the largest collection of books in the ancient world.
105043.m: Eratosthenes ran the Library of Alexandria.

105044.q: What do you find with the sieve of Eratosthenes?
105044.e: You cross out all the multiples of 2, 3, 5 and so on, one after another. What is left are the prime numbers.
105044.m: The sieve of Eratosthenes sorts out the prime numbers.

105045.q: How many prime numbers are left between 1 and 20 in the sieve of Eratosthenes?
105045.e: What is left is 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17 and 19. That is 8 numbers.
105045.m: There are eight prime numbers between 1 and 20.

105046.q: Eratosthenes is regarded as the founder of which science, whose name he is said to have coined?
105046.e: Eratosthenes wrote a work describing the Earth. The term geography is attributed to him.
105046.m: Eratosthenes is regarded as the founder of geography.

105047.q: Which nickname did critics give Eratosthenes because he was considered second best in many subjects?
105047.e: Beta is the second letter of the Greek alphabet. The nickname hinted that he was good at everything but rarely the best.

105048.q: What subject are Euclid's “Elements” mainly about?
105048.e: The Elements sum up the mathematical knowledge of the Greeks, especially geometry. They begin with points, straight lines and circles.
105048.m: Euclid's Elements are a basic book of geometry.

105049.q: In which city did Euclid work around 300 BC?
105049.e: Euclid taught in Alexandria, which was then a centre of science. Little else is known about his life.

a: He proved theorems from a few basic principles
He told myths about the gods
105050.e: Euclid began with definitions and basic principles that he did not need to prove. From these he worked out all the other theorems step by step.
105050.m: Euclid derived all his theorems logically from basic principles.

105051.q: Which postulate in Euclid's “Elements” was disputed for a long time?
105051.e: The parallel postulate is about how parallel lines behave. Many people tried in vain to prove it from the other principles.
105051.m: The parallel postulate kept mathematicians busy for two thousand years.

105052.q: What is the highest common factor of 48 and 18?
105052.e: 48 ÷ 18 leaves a remainder of 12, 18 ÷ 12 leaves a remainder of 6, and 12 ÷ 6 leaves a remainder of 0. So the highest common factor is 6.
105052.m: The highest common factor of 48 and 18 is 6.

105053.q: What is the name of the great work by Pliny the Elder?
105053.e: The Naturalis historia, in English Natural History, collects knowledge about nature, animals, plants and rocks. It was widely read in ancient times.
105053.m: Pliny the Elder wrote the Naturalis historia.

105054.q: What did Pliny the Elder write about in his “Naturalis historia”?
105054.e: The Natural History has 37 books and collects knowledge about nature, animals, plants, rocks and much more.

105055.q: In which event did Pliny the Elder die in AD 79?
105055.e: During the eruption of Vesuvius, Pliny wanted to help people and observe the natural event. He died on the coast near Stabiae.
105055.m: Pliny the Elder died in the eruption of Vesuvius.

105056.q: Why did Pliny the Elder sail to the coast with ships during the eruption of Vesuvius?
a: To help people and observe the eruption
To flee from the Germanic tribes
105056.e: Pliny commanded the Roman fleet at Misenum. He wanted to rescue people and see the natural event close up.
105056.m: Pliny wanted to help and observe during the eruption of Vesuvius.

105057.q: Who described the death of Pliny the Elder in letters to the historian Tacitus?
105057.e: Pliny the Younger experienced the eruption from a distance. In two letters to Tacitus he described the events.
105057.m: Pliny the Younger reported on the eruption of Vesuvius.

105058.q: What are particularly violent, explosive volcanic eruptions called today?
105058.e: The name recalls Pliny the Younger, who described the eruption of AD 79 in detail. A tall column of ash and gas is typical.
105058.m: Plinian eruptions hurl tall columns of ash into the sky.

105059.q: In which language did Pliny the Elder write?
105059.e: Pliny was a Roman and wrote in Latin. He also used many Greek sources for his work.
105059.m: Pliny the Elder wrote in Latin.

105060.q: What is the “Naturalis historia” often regarded as today?
105060.e: Pliny collected knowledge from thousands of sources on a great many topics. That is why his work is regarded as a kind of early encyclopedia.
105060.m: Pliny's Natural History is regarded as an early encyclopedia.

105061.q: In which present-day town near the Swiss border was Pliny the Elder born?
105061.e: Pliny was born around AD 23 in Novum Comum. That is today's Como on Lake Como, not far from Ticino.
105061.m: Pliny the Elder came from Como.

105062.q: Around how many axes can a hinge joint move?
105062.e: A hinge joint only moves around a single cross axis. That is why it can only bend and straighten.
105062.m: A hinge joint has only one axis of movement.

105063.q: Which joint works like a hinge joint?
a: The upper ankle joint of the foot
The joint between the head and the first neck vertebra
105063.e: In the upper ankle joint you raise and lower your foot. This movement around one axis is typical of a hinge joint.
105063.m: The upper ankle joint raises and lowers the foot like a hinge.

105064.q: Which finger joints are hinge joints?
a: Only the knuckle joints at the base
All joints up to the shoulder
105064.e: The joints between the finger bones can only bend and straighten. They hardly move sideways.
105064.m: The middle and end joints of the fingers are hinge joints.

105065.q: Which part of the elbow works as a hinge joint?
a: The joint between the humerus and the ulna
The joint between the ulna and the radius
The joint between the shoulder blade and the upper arm
The joint between the radius and the wrist
105065.e: The elbow is made up of three joints. Bending and straightening happen between the humerus and the ulna.
105065.m: The humerus and ulna form the hinge of the elbow.

105066.q: Why is the knee joint often called a rotating hinge joint?
a: When the knee is bent, the lower leg can turn a little
The kneecap keeps spinning in circles
The knee can circle in every direction
The thigh turns 360 degrees in the knee
105066.e: The knee mainly bends and straightens like a hinge. When it is bent, the lower leg can also turn a little inwards and outwards.
105066.m: The bent knee allows a small turn as well as bending.

105067.q: What stops you bending your straightened elbow further backwards?
105067.e: The olecranon is the upper end of the ulna, the point of the elbow. When you straighten the arm, it locks into a hollow in the humerus and stops the movement.
105067.m: When you straighten the arm, the olecranon stops the elbow like a buffer.

105068.q: Which muscles work as opponents at a hinge joint like the elbow?
a: Two flexors on the same side
A chewing muscle and a neck muscle
A heart muscle and a skeletal muscle
105068.e: At the elbow the biceps bends and the triceps straightens. Muscles can only pull, so each direction needs its own muscle.
105068.m: A flexor and an extensor move a hinge joint in opposite directions.

105069.q: Which joint is not a hinge joint?
a: The joint between the humerus and the ulna
105069.e: The shoulder joint is a ball and socket joint and moves in many directions. The other joints can only bend and straighten.
105069.m: The shoulder joint is a ball and socket joint, not a hinge joint.

105070.q: Around how many main axes can a saddle joint move?
105070.e: The two saddle-shaped joint surfaces allow movement around two axes, for example forwards and back and to the side with the thumb.
105070.m: A saddle joint moves around two main axes.

105071.q: Where is the best-known saddle joint in the human body?
a: At the base of the thumb
105071.e: The thumb’s saddle joint lies between the wrist and the thumb’s metacarpal. It makes the thumb especially flexible.
105071.m: The thumb’s saddle joint is at the base of the thumb.

105072.q: Which important thumb movement does the saddle joint make possible?
a: Bringing the thumb opposite the other fingers
Spinning the thumb all the way round
Folding the thumb back to the forearm
105072.e: Thanks to the saddle joint, the thumb can touch the fingertips. This is called opposition and makes gripping possible.
105072.m: The saddle joint lets the thumb face the fingers so we can grip.

105073.q: Where does the saddle joint get its name from?
a: The joint surfaces are curved like a riding saddle
It was first discovered in horses
You mainly need it for riding
It sits like a saddle on the spine
105073.e: Both joint surfaces curve upwards in one direction and downwards in the other. They sit crosswise on each other like a rider on a saddle.
105073.m: The joint surfaces of a saddle joint look like a riding saddle.

105074.q: What is arthritis (osteoarthritis) in the thumb’s saddle joint?
a: Wear and tear of the joint at the base of the thumb
A skin disease of the hand
105074.e: With osteoarthritis, the cartilage in the joint wears away. People with it often have pain when opening jars or writing.
105074.m: Osteoarthritis means wear and tear of a joint.

105075.q: Which movement can a ball and socket joint make that a saddle joint hardly can?
a: Turning around its own long axis
105075.e: A ball and socket joint has three axes and can also rotate. The saddle joint has only two main axes.
105075.m: A ball and socket joint can rotate; a saddle joint hardly can.

105076.q: Why is the thumb’s saddle joint so important for humans?
a: It allows the precision grip between thumb and index finger
It carries the body’s weight when standing
It protects the nerves in the forearm
It moves the wrist when waving
105076.e: With the precision grip we hold small things such as a needle or a pencil. For this the thumb must be able to move freely towards the fingers.
105076.m: Without the thumb’s saddle joint we couldn’t grip small things precisely.

105077.q: Around which axis does a pivot joint move?
a: Around a cross axis like a hinge
105077.e: In a pivot joint, a bone turns around its own long axis, much like a wheel around its axle.
105077.m: A pivot joint turns a bone around its long axis.

105078.q: Which pivot joint do you need to turn your head left and right?
a: The joint between the top neck vertebrae
105078.e: The first neck vertebra turns together with the head around a peg on the second neck vertebra. That way you can turn your head to the side.
105078.m: The top neck vertebrae form a pivot joint for the head.

105079.q: Which pivot joint lets you turn your palm up and down?
a: The joint between the radius and the ulna
The joint between the upper arm and the shoulder blade
105079.e: When you turn your hand, the radius turns around the ulna. The joints between these two bones are pivot joints.
105079.m: The radius and ulna form the pivot joints of the forearm.

105080.q: In which everyday movement does the pivot joint in the forearm work?
a: Turning a key in a lock
105080.e: When you turn a key, the radius turns around the ulna. The pivot joints in the forearm make this possible.
105080.m: When you turn a key, the pivot joints in the forearm are working.

105081.q: Which movement does a pivot joint make possible?
105081.e: In a pivot joint, a bone turns around its long axis, a bit like a doorknob. Circling in every direction is what a ball and socket joint can do.
105081.m: A pivot joint allows a turning movement.

105082.q: What holds the head of the radius in its pivot joint at the elbow?
105082.e: The annular ligament wraps around the head of the radius like a ring. That way the radius can turn inside it without slipping out.
105082.m: A ring ligament holds the head of the radius at the elbow.

105083.q: Which forearm bone turns around the other when you turn your hand over?
105083.e: The ulna stays almost still during the turn. The radius crosses over the ulna and takes the hand with it.
105083.m: When you turn your hand, it is mainly the radius that moves.

105084.q: What other name is used for a pivot joint?
105084.e: Pivot joints are also called wheel joints or trochoid joints, because one part turns like a wheel or around a peg.
105084.m: A pivot joint is also called a wheel joint or trochoid joint.

105085.q: What shape are the joint surfaces of an ellipsoid (egg-shaped) joint?
a: An oval head lies in an oval socket
A ball lies in a round socket
A roller lies in a groove
Two flat discs lie on top of each other
105085.e: The head of the joint is long and oval like an egg and fits into a socket of the same shape. That is where the name comes from.
105085.m: In an ellipsoid joint, an egg-shaped head sits in an oval socket.

105086.q: Around how many axes can an ellipsoid joint move?
105086.e: An ellipsoid joint allows movements around two axes, for example forwards and back and to the side.
105086.m: An ellipsoid joint has two axes of movement.

105087.q: Which joint in the hand is an ellipsoid joint?
a: The joint between the radius and the wrist bones
The joint between the ulna and the upper arm
105087.e: The upper wrist joint connects the radius with the wrist bones. Its joint surfaces are oval.
105087.m: The joint between the radius and the wrist bones is an ellipsoid joint.

105088.q: Which movements does the ellipsoid joint in the wrist allow?
a: Bending and straightening plus tilting to the side
Circling around all axes and rotating
105088.e: You can bend your hand up and down and tilt it towards the thumb or little finger side. Rotating, on the other hand, is not possible in an ellipsoid joint.
105088.m: In the wrist’s ellipsoid joint you can bend, straighten and tilt sideways.

105089.q: Why can’t an ellipsoid joint turn around its own axis?
a: The oval head jams in the oval socket
It has grown together with bone
There are no muscles for it
105089.e: An egg-shaped head only fits into the long socket in one position. If you turn it, it gets stuck.
105089.m: The oval shape stops an ellipsoid joint from rotating.

105090.q: What else is the egg-shaped joint called?
105090.e: An ellipse is an oval. That is why the egg-shaped joint is also called an ellipsoid joint.
105090.m: The egg-shaped joint is also called an ellipsoid joint.

105091.q: Which head movement does the ellipsoid joint between the skull and the first neck vertebra make possible?
105091.e: The upper head joint is an ellipsoid joint. It mainly allows nodding and slight tilting of the head to the side.
105091.m: The ellipsoid joint below the skull allows nodding.

105092.q: What wraps a true joint like a closed tube?
105092.e: The joint capsule surrounds the whole joint and seals the joint space tightly.
105092.m: The joint capsule wraps a true joint like a tube.

105093.q: Which two layers make up the joint capsule?
a: An outer fibrous layer and an inner joint lining
105093.e: The tough outer fibrous layer gives support. The delicate inner layer, the joint lining, lines the inside of the joint.
105093.m: The joint capsule has a tough outer layer and a delicate inner lining.

105094.q: Which layer of the joint capsule makes the joint lubricant?
105094.e: The joint lining, also called the synovial membrane, releases the fluid into the joint space.
105094.m: The joint lining makes the joint lubricant.

105095.q: In medical language, what does the ending “-itis” mean in words such as bronchitis or arthritis?
105095.e: In medicine the ending “-itis” means inflammation. An inflammation of the joint lining, for example, is called synovitis.
105095.m: The ending “-itis” stands for an inflammation.

105096.q: What strengthens the joint capsule from the outside and makes the joint stable?
105096.e: Many ligaments are woven into the joint capsule or lie right against it. They prevent too much movement.
105096.m: Ligaments strengthen the joint capsule from the outside.

105097.q: What is the narrow space between the cartilage surfaces inside the joint capsule called?
105097.e: The joint space is filled with joint fluid. On an X-ray you see it as a dark gap between the bones.
105097.m: The joint space lies between the cartilage surfaces.

105098.q: What do you call connections between bones with no joint space and no joint capsule?
105098.e: In false joints, the bones are joined directly by cartilage or connective tissue, for example at the pubic symphysis. They can hardly move.
105098.m: False joints have no joint space and no capsule.

105099.q: How do you know with your eyes closed whether your arm is bent?
a: Sensors in joints and muscles report it to the brain
105099.e: Tiny sensors for position and movement sit in the joint capsule, ligaments and muscles. They constantly send messages to the brain.
105099.m: Sensors in the joint capsule tell the brain where the joints are.

a: In the joint space between the bones
105100.e: Joint fluid fills the narrow space between the cartilage surfaces of a joint. There it works like a lubricant.
105100.m: The joint fluid is in the joint space.

105101.q: Because of its sticky texture, what substance does joint fluid remind people of?
105101.e: Joint fluid is clear and stringy like egg white. Its technical name, synovia, probably contains the Latin word “ovum” for egg.
105101.m: Joint fluid is sticky and clear like raw egg white.

105102.q: Which substance makes the joint fluid especially thick and sticky?
105102.e: Hyaluronic acid binds a lot of water and makes the fluid slimy. This lets the cartilage surfaces glide with almost no friction.
105102.m: Hyaluronic acid makes joint fluid thick and slippery.

105103.q: Why is joint fluid vital for the joint cartilage?
a: The cartilage has no blood vessels and is nourished by it
105103.e: Joint cartilage has no blood vessels of its own. It gets nutrients from the joint fluid.
105103.m: Joint cartilage is nourished by the joint fluid.

105104.q: Why is regular exercise good for cartilage?
a: Pressure and release pump nutrients into the cartilage
Exercise makes the joint fluid thinner
105104.e: Cartilage works like a sponge. Under load, fluid is squeezed out; when the load is released, it soaks up fresh joint fluid with nutrients.
105104.m: Exercise pumps nutrients into cartilage like a sponge.

105105.q: What do you call an abnormal build-up of fluid in a joint?
105105.e: After injuries or with inflammation, too much fluid often forms. The joint then swells up and feels tight.
105105.m: A joint effusion is too much fluid in the joint.

105106.q: What is the test called in which joint fluid is taken out with a needle?
105106.e: In an aspiration, the doctor inserts a fine needle into the joint. The fluid is examined, for example for bacteria or blood.
105106.m: In a joint aspiration, joint fluid is taken out with a needle.

105107.q: What does healthy joint fluid look like?
105107.e: Healthy joint fluid is see-through and slightly yellowish. Cloudy or bloody fluid points to inflammation or an injury.
105107.m: Healthy joint fluid is clear and pale yellow.

105108.q: What is a meniscus in the knee made of?
105108.e: Menisci are made of fibrocartilage. It is firm yet elastic and can absorb pressure well.
105108.m: A meniscus is made of elastic fibrocartilage.

105109.q: What does the Greek word “meniscus” mean?
105109.e: The menisci are curved like a half moon. That is why they were given the name “little moon”.
105109.m: Meniscus means “little moon” because it is shaped like a crescent moon.

105110.q: Which meniscus tears much more often?
105110.e: The inner meniscus is attached to the inner ligament and cannot move out of the way as easily. That is why it tears more often.
105110.m: The inner meniscus tears more often than the outer meniscus.

105111.q: During which movement does a meniscus tear especially easily?
a: Twisting on a bent knee that is carrying weight
105111.e: If you twist with your knee bent and your whole weight on it, the meniscus gets trapped between the bones. This often happens in football or skiing.
105111.m: Twisting on a bent knee is dangerous for the meniscus.

105112.q: Which method is usually used today to operate on a torn meniscus?
a: A large cut right across the knee
105112.e: In keyhole surgery, called arthroscopy, a camera and fine instruments are inserted into the knee through small cuts.
105112.m: A torn meniscus is usually operated on with keyhole surgery.

105113.q: Why does a tear in the inner part of the meniscus heal poorly?
a: This part has hardly any blood supply
This part is made of bone
This part has too many nerves
This part lies outside the knee
105113.e: Only the outer edge of the meniscus has blood vessels. The inner area lacks the nutrients needed for healing.
105113.m: The inner part of the meniscus has hardly any blood supply and heals poorly.

105114.q: Between which bones do the menisci lie?
a: Between the thigh bone and the shin bone
Between the kneecap and the fibula
Between the shin bone and the heel bone
Between the hip bone and the thigh bone
105114.e: The menisci sit on top of the shin bone. The rounded ends of the thigh bone roll and glide on them.
105114.m: The menisci lie between the thigh bone and the shin bone.

105115.q: Apart from cushioning, what job do the menisci have?
a: They enlarge the contact area and spread the pressure
105115.e: The rounded ends of the thigh bone do not fit well on the flat shin bone. The menisci fill the gap, so the load is spread over a larger area.
105115.m: Menisci spread the pressure in the knee over a larger area.

105116.q: Which cruciate ligament tears much more often?
105116.e: The anterior (front) cruciate ligament is under heavy strain when you twist or stop suddenly. Tearing it is one of the most common serious knee injuries in sport.
105116.m: The anterior cruciate ligament tears much more often than the posterior one.

105117.q: Which movement does the anterior cruciate ligament prevent?
105117.e: The anterior cruciate ligament runs at an angle from the shin bone backwards and upwards to the thigh bone. This stops the shin bone from sliding forwards.
105117.m: The anterior cruciate ligament stops the lower leg from sliding forwards.

105118.q: How does a doctor check whether the anterior cruciate ligament is torn?
a: She carefully pulls the lower leg forwards
She taps the heel with a hammer
She listens to the knee with a stethoscope
105118.e: If the shin bone can be pulled unusually far forwards, the anterior cruciate ligament is no longer holding. Often an MRI scan is done as well.
105118.m: A loose shin bone shows a torn cruciate ligament.

105119.q: In which sport, popular in Switzerland, are especially many cruciate ligaments torn?
105119.e: When skiing, the skis can twist the knee while the body keeps moving. Football also causes many cruciate ligament tears.
105119.m: Skiing and football are typical sports for cruciate ligament tears.

105120.q: In an operation, what is a torn cruciate ligament often replaced with?
a: A piece of the patient’s own tendon
105120.e: Often a tendon from the thigh or part of the kneecap tendon is used. It is anchored in the knee as a new ligament.
105120.m: A new cruciate ligament is often made from the body’s own tendon.

105121.q: What do people often notice at the moment a cruciate ligament tears?
a: An audible pop in the knee
105121.e: Many people report a bang or pop in the knee. Afterwards the knee usually swells quickly and feels unstable.
105121.m: A cruciate ligament tear is often noticed as a pop in the knee.

105122.q: What helps athletes prevent a cruciate ligament tear?
a: Strong leg muscles and a good warm-up
Only doing sport in the evening
105122.e: Strong thighs and calves support the knee. If you warm up and land jumps cleanly, you twist your knee less often.
105122.m: Strong leg muscles protect the cruciate ligaments.

105123.q: How many cruciate ligaments does a knee joint have?
105123.e: Each knee has an anterior (front) and a posterior (back) cruciate ligament. Together they keep the knee stable forwards and backwards.
105123.m: Each knee has a front and a back cruciate ligament.

105124.q: Unlike a tendon, what does a ligament connect?
105124.e: Ligaments hold bones together at joints. Tendons, on the other hand, pass the force from a muscle to a bone.
105124.m: Ligaments connect bones, tendons connect muscles to bones.

105125.q: What are ligaments mainly made of?
a: Tough connective tissue with collagen fibres
105125.e: Ligaments are made of tightly packed collagen fibres. They are very strong when pulled but only stretch a little.
105125.m: Ligaments are made of strong collagen fibres.

105126.q: How is a torn outer ankle ligament usually treated today?
a: Without surgery, with a splint and physiotherapy
With a plaster cast for a whole year
Not at all, you must keep training straight away
105126.e: Most torn outer ankle ligaments heal well with a supporting splint and targeted exercises. An operation is rarely needed.
105126.m: A torn outer ankle ligament usually heals without surgery.

105127.q: What can happen if a torn ligament heals badly?
a: An unstable joint that keeps giving way
A stiff joint that can never bend again
105127.e: If a ligament stays too long or loose, it no longer holds the joint properly. You then twist it again more easily.
105127.m: A badly healed ligament can make the joint unstable.

105128.q: Roughly how long does a torn ligament take until it can carry weight again?
105128.e: Ligaments have a poor blood supply and heal slowly. It usually takes around six weeks or longer until they hold well again.
105128.m: A torn ligament needs around six weeks to heal.

105129.q: What is the technical term for a dislocated joint?
105129.e: In a luxation, the joint surfaces lose contact with each other. A fracture, on the other hand, is a broken bone.
105129.m: A luxation is a dislocated joint.

105130.q: What is the technical term for putting a dislocated joint back in place?
105130.e: In a reduction, the doctor puts the head of the joint back into its socket, often with painkillers.
105130.m: A reduction puts the joint back in its place.

105131.q: What is it called when a joint is only partly dislocated?
105131.e: In a subluxation, the joint surfaces still partly touch. Often the joint pops back by itself.
105131.m: In a subluxation the joint is only partly dislocated.

105132.q: Which joint easily dislocates in toddlers if they are pulled up sharply by the arm?
a: The head of the radius at the elbow
105132.e: In small children the head of the radius still sits loosely in its holder. A sudden jerk makes it slip partly out, and the child then keeps the arm still.
105132.m: Never pull toddlers up sharply by the arm, or the head of the radius can slip out.

105133.q: In which direction does the kneecap almost always move when it dislocates?
105133.e: The pull of the thigh muscles draws the kneecap slightly outwards. That is why it almost always dislocates to the outer side.
105133.m: When it dislocates, the kneecap usually moves outwards.

105134.q: Why should you not put a dislocated joint back yourself?
a: You could injure nerves, blood vessels or bones
The joint will never go back in
It is forbidden to give first aid
105134.e: Nerves and blood vessels often run next to the joint. There may also be a fracture that only shows up on an X-ray.
105134.m: A dislocated joint needs a doctor.

105135.q: Which parts of a joint are often injured as well in a dislocation?
105135.e: For the bone to jump out of its socket, the capsule and ligaments must be strongly stretched or torn.
105135.m: In a dislocation, the capsule and ligaments often tear too.

105136.q: Why does a shoulder dislocate more easily again after the first time?
a: The capsule and ligaments stay stretched or torn
The upper arm bone gets longer
105136.e: If the injured supporting tissues do not heal tightly together, the joint is less stable. This is common, especially in young people.
105136.m: After a first shoulder dislocation, the joint is often less stable.

105137.q: What happens in a joint with osteoarthritis?
a: The bones become as soft as rubber
105137.e: Osteoarthritis is wear and tear of the joint. The cartilage becomes thinner and cracked until bone can rub on bone.
105137.m: In osteoarthritis, the joint cartilage wears away.

105138.q: What does the ending “-itis” in the word arthritis mean?
105138.e: Arthritis is an inflammation of a joint, osteoarthritis is wear and tear. The two are often confused.

105139.q: In which people does osteoarthritis occur most often?
105139.e: Osteoarthritis is joint wear that develops over many years. That is why it mainly affects older people.

a: A smooth layer on the ends of the bones in a joint
A muscle that moves the joint
A ligament that connects two bones
A fluid in the bone marrow
105140.e: Joint cartilage covers the ends of the bones and makes sure they glide smoothly over each other. In osteoarthritis it wears away.
105140.m: Joint cartilage lets the bones in a joint glide.

105141.q: Which risk factor puts strain on knees and hips and encourages osteoarthritis?
105141.e: Every extra kilogram presses on the joints with every step. That is why being overweight speeds up cartilage wear.
105141.m: Being overweight strains the joints and encourages osteoarthritis.

105142.q: What is a typical early sign of osteoarthritis?
a: Pain in the first steps after a rest
A joint that is always cold
105142.e: This is called start-up pain. After a few minutes of movement it often gets better.
105142.m: Start-up pain after a rest is a typical sign of osteoarthritis.

105143.q: What can often be seen on an X-ray in osteoarthritis?
a: A joint space that has become narrower
105143.e: Cartilage does not show up on an X-ray. When it gets thinner, the bones move closer together and the gap between them looks narrower.
105143.m: A narrow joint space on an X-ray points to osteoarthritis.

105144.q: Which sports are often recommended for osteoarthritis in the knee or hip?
105144.e: These sports move the joints evenly without hard jolts. That keeps muscles and cartilage in good shape.
105144.m: Cycling and swimming are gentle on joints with osteoarthritis.

105145.q: Which two parts of the hip joint does a total hip replacement replace?
a: The hip socket and the head of the thigh bone
The kneecap and the top of the shin bone
The meniscus and the cruciate ligament
105145.e: In a total hip replacement, an artificial socket is placed in the pelvis. A stem with a ball replaces the head of the thigh bone.
105145.m: A total hip replacement replaces the socket and head of the hip joint.

105146.q: What is the most common reason for a hip replacement?
105146.e: When the cartilage is badly damaged, every step hurts. An artificial joint can then take away the pain and improve movement.
105146.m: Most hip replacements are done because of osteoarthritis.

105147.q: Which metal are many implant stems that sit in the thigh bone made of?
105147.e: Titanium is light, very strong and well tolerated by the body. The bone can even grow onto its surface.
105147.m: Many implant stems are made of well-tolerated titanium.

a: A plaster cast for the leg
105148.e: In a hip replacement, surgeons replace the diseased hip joint with an artificial one made of metal, ceramic or plastic.
105148.m: A hip replacement is an artificial hip joint.

105149.q: In which two ways is a hip replacement fixed in the bone?
a: With bone cement or by growing in without cement
With screws from outside through the skin
Only by muscles, with no fixing at all
105149.e: Cemented implants are firm straight away. With cement-free implants, the bone grows into the rough surface.
105149.m: Hip replacements are either cemented or grow into the bone without cement.

105150.q: What does the prefix “endo” in the word endoprosthesis mean?
105150.e: An endoprosthesis is placed inside the body. An artificial leg that is fitted from outside, on the other hand, is an exoprosthesis.
105150.m: An endoprosthesis sits inside the body.

105151.q: In many cases, how long does a modern hip replacement last?
a: Always only until the next winter
105151.e: Thanks to good materials, many hip replacements work for decades. If one becomes loose, it can be replaced.
105151.m: Many hip replacements last twenty years or longer.

105152.q: What material is the artificial head of the hip or the gliding surface of the socket often made of?
105152.e: Ceramic is very hard and smooth, and a special plastic called polyethylene glides well. This means little wear.
105152.m: The hip head and socket are often made of smooth ceramic or plastic.

105153.q: Which complication is especially feared in the first weeks after a hip replacement?
105153.e: Until the muscles and capsule have healed, the artificial head can jump out of the socket. That is why extreme movements are avoided at first.
105153.m: After the operation you must avoid extreme hip movements so the implant does not dislocate.

105154.q: Which animals can also place their thumb opposite their other fingers?
105154.e: Many monkeys and apes also have an opposable thumb. In humans, however, it is especially long and flexible.
105154.m: Many monkeys and apes can also place their thumb opposite their fingers.

105155.q: Which joint can move more, an ellipsoid joint or a ball-and-socket joint?
105155.e: A ball-and-socket joint like the shoulder moves around three axes and can also rotate. An ellipsoid joint has only two axes.
105155.m: A ball-and-socket joint can move more than an ellipsoid joint.

105156.q: What can help with severe osteoarthritis in the knee or hip when nothing else works?
105156.e: If the joint is badly worn, it can be replaced by an implant made of metal and plastic. Afterwards the pain is usually much less.
105156.m: An artificial joint can help with severe osteoarthritis.

105157.q: How can you often tell from the outside that a shoulder is dislocated?
a: The shoulder looks angular with a dent
The shoulder turns completely blue and cold
The shoulder becomes as soft as rubber
105157.e: When the head of the upper arm bone jumps out of the socket, the round shape of the shoulder is missing. A hollow forms below the top of the shoulder.
105157.m: A dislocated shoulder often looks angular and has a dent.

105158.q: What can happen if a torn-off piece of meniscus gets trapped in the knee?
a: Suddenly the knee can no longer be fully straightened
The knee becomes longer for good
The foot goes to sleep for ever
105158.e: The loose piece catches between the bones and blocks the joint. This is called a locked joint.
105158.m: A trapped piece of meniscus can lock the knee.

105159.q: What is a ligament injury called when the ligament is only overstretched but not torn?
105159.e: In a sprain the fibres are overstretched but still whole. It usually heals faster than a tear.
105159.m: A sprained ligament is overstretched but not torn.

105160.q: Which ligament in the knee is injured especially often when skiing?
105160.e: In a fall, the knee often bends inwards while the ski turns outwards. This overstretches or tears the ligament on the inside of the knee.
105160.m: When skiing, the inner ligament of the knee is often injured.

105161.q: Which imaging method shows torn ligaments especially well?
105161.e: An MRI shows soft tissues such as ligaments, cartilage and menisci very precisely. An X-ray, on the other hand, mainly shows bones.
105161.m: Ligaments show up well on an MRI, bones on an X-ray.

105162.q: Apart from heaviness, which property of an object does mass describe?
105162.e: The greater the mass, the harder it is to set an object in motion or slow it down. This property is called inertia.
105162.m: An object with a large mass also has a lot of inertia.

105163.q: How many milligrams are in one gram?
105163.e: The prefix “milli” means one thousandth. So 1 g equals 1000 mg.
105163.m: One gram has a thousand milligrams.

105164.m: To convert kilograms into grams, multiply by a thousand.

105165.q: How does the mass of an ice cube change when it melts completely?
105165.e: When it melts, only the state changes. No water particles are lost, so the mass stays the same.
105165.m: Mass stays the same when something melts.

105166.q: Which symbol is used for mass in physics?
105166.e: The small m stands for mass. g stands for gravitational field strength and F for a force.
105166.m: The symbol for mass is a small m.

105167.q: Three packs of butter each have a mass of 250 g. What is their total mass?
105167.e: Masses can be added: 3 · 250 g = 750 g.
105167.m: You can add the masses of several objects together.

105168.m: Divide grams by a thousand to get kilograms.

105169.q: In which special unit is the mass of gemstones often given?
105169.e: One carat equals 0.2 g. This unit is used for diamonds and other gemstones.
105169.m: The mass of gemstones is measured in carats.

105170.q: In which unit is weight measured?
105170.e: Weight is a force. Forces are measured in newtons, N for short.

105171.q: How do you calculate the weight of an object?
105171.e: Weight equals mass times gravitational field strength, so F = m · g.
105171.m: Weight is the product of mass and gravitational field strength.

105172.q: What is the weight of a child with a mass of 45 kg in Switzerland (field strength 9.81 N/kg)?
105172.e: F = 45 kg · 9.81 N/kg = 441.45 N, so about 441 N.
105172.m: The weight in newtons is about ten times the number of kilograms.

105173.q: Which device measures a weight directly?
105173.e: A newton meter contains a spring that stretches under the load. You read off the force in newtons on the scale.
105173.m: A newton meter shows weight in newtons.

105174.q: How does the weight of an object change if you double its mass in the same place?
105174.e: Weight is mass times field strength. If the place stays the same, it grows in the same proportion as the mass.
105174.m: Twice the mass means twice the weight in the same place.

105175.q: An object has a weight of 30 N on Earth. What is its mass if you use 10 N/kg?
105175.e: m = F ÷ g = 30 N ÷ 10 N/kg = 3 kg.
105175.m: You get the mass by dividing the weight by the field strength.

105176.q: What do bathroom scales actually measure?
a: The weight, which they convert into kilograms
The mass directly, regardless of location
105176.e: The scales measure how hard you press on them. They convert this value into kilograms using the Earth's field strength.

105177.q: Why do astronauts float in the ISS space station?
a: They are constantly falling round the Earth together with the station
There is no gravity at all in space
The station pushes them up with air
105177.e: Even at a height of 400 km the Earth still pulls strongly. But the station and the people fall round the Earth together, so they feel no weight.
105177.m: In the space station you float because everything falls round the Earth together.

105178.q: Two children of 35 kg and 40 kg sit on a bench. What weight do they exert on the bench together (10 N/kg)?
105178.e: Together they have 75 kg. F = 75 kg · 10 N/kg = 750 N.
105178.m: The weights of several objects can be added together.

105179.q: Roughly what is the gravitational field strength in Switzerland?
105179.e: In central Europe the field strength is about 9.81 N/kg. In lessons people often simplify it to 10 N/kg.
105179.m: In Switzerland the field strength is about 9.81 N/kg.

105180.q: Where is the gravitational field strength much greater than on Earth?
a: At the surface of the Sun
On the summit of Mount Everest
105180.e: The Sun has an enormous mass. At its surface, almost thirty times more force acts on each kilogram than on Earth. On the Moon and Mars the field strength is smaller.
105180.m: At the Sun's surface the field strength is almost thirty times that on Earth.

105181.q: Why is the gravitational field strength smaller at the equator than at the poles?
a: The Earth is wider there and spins faster
It is warmer at the equator
There is more water at the equator
The air is thinner at the equator
105181.e: The Earth bulges slightly at the equator, so you stand further from the centre. Also, the Earth's rotation pushes outwards most strongly there.
105181.m: The Earth's flattening and rotation make the field strength smaller at the equator.

105182.q: Which unit is the unit N/kg equal to?
105182.e: One newton is 1 kg · m/s². Dividing by kg leaves m/s². That is why the field strength equals the acceleration due to gravity.
105182.m: Field strength in N/kg is the same as the acceleration due to gravity in m/s².

105183.q: On which planet in our solar system is the gravitational field strength at the surface greatest?
